utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kirudja, yesterday we left off discussing a question I had asked you with respect to your knowledge about the presence of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not sure that I remembered your answer. Did you say you knew about their presence or not, and how far they were there or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't know the matters which you put to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that, apart from the fact that you had your own personal knowledge, that you also took care as to what was being written in the UN Secretary-General reports, what they said. So let me remind you, and I'm quoting, that there's the UN Security Council report, the title: Report by the UN Secretary-General Pursuant to the 749 UN Security Council Resolution, 1992, the 13th of May. The 13th of May, yes, 1992. That's the date. The English version, UN Secretary-General Report Pursuant to the Resolution I've just quoted, and he says in that document, in chapter 2, the following: "2.4 But there is no doubt that certain members of the Croatian army with their weapons are deployed in Herzegovina and Bosanska Krupa near Bihac in the north-west, around Bosanski Brod to the north-east and in Eastern Bosnia as well and that they are deployed en masse." Do you recall that? I assume that, as a UN employee, as a UN official, you must have read those reports by the UN Secretary-General which referred to the territory you yourself were working in.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In general, reports of the Secretary-General in the area we were concerned would have information that I would have knowledge of, if not directly -- or, let me say the United Nations Protection Force was deployed in the -- in a number locations in the former Yugoslavia, and the reports of the Secretary-General, as you would appreciate, would encompass sources of information that were reflective of the entire information reaching the Secretary-General from all parts of the nation. Therefore, while in general I would know of those reports, I wouldn't be the person you would want to question on the details contained therein in a given report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in view of the questions related to the JNA, I'm going to quote the next point from this same report. It is point 5 in that same chapter, the one I mentioned, in which he says the following: "Further concern was caused by the decision made by the Belgrade authorities up until the 18th of May to have all members of the JNA pull out of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are not citizens of that republic. This will leave Bosnia-Herzegovina without any effective control, 50.000 Serb forces will be pulled out and their weapons." Do you remember that portion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Milosevic, I don't have that report directly in front of me, but I can recognise certain points you have made. For example, the sentence about -- about Belgrade -- by the decision made by the Belgrade authorities up until the 18th of May to have all members of the JNA pull out of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are not citizens of that republic. I have testified directly to knowing that information. Not from the Secretary-General's report only. It's the other way around; from the ground where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, that's very good. That means that you know that from your own personal knowledge. And this report goes on to say on page 10, under chapter 5, it says, "Comments," this is the Comments section. Do you know about this event: "The Muslim forces on the 3rd of May, violating the agreement on safe passage for members of the JNA which were leaving the headquarters in Sarajevo in cold blood killed a certain number of soldiers belonging to the JNA in the persons of high-ranking UNPROFOR officers who were powerless to prevent this massacre." So the term "massacre" is used, and that was the 3rd of May, while they were withdrawing. In the presence of UNPROFOR. That's when this massacre took place, the massacre of a number of JNA soldiers. Do you happen to recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, my testimony contains reference to General Spiro Nikovic speaking to us, I think a day or two after the reports of that incident were -- had reached our part of the sector. My testimony reflects somewhere in this document that you may have Mr. Spiro -- General Spiro Nikovic knew of that. He apprised us of that, and I recall mentioning it had coloured his mood that day. He was not his jovial self because of the incident. I have testified to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see now, there's also this, a report to the UN Security Council. It says Security Council here. Distribution is general, S/24049 of the 30th of May, the original is in English. And then it goes on to state the following: "The present report is remitted to the secretary -- to the Security Council pursuant to paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752, 1992." And then in the first paragraph where it says Background, point 2, it states the following: [In English] [Previous translation continues]... "13th of May 1992 President Izetbegovic of Bosnia-Herzegovina met at Skopje with General Blagojevic, Chief of Staff of JNA, Yugoslav federal army, and acting Federal Secretary of Defence and Mr. Branko Kostic, vice-president of the Federal Presidency in Belgrade, to define the role of JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina and it's eventual withdrawal. This meeting did not produce a definite agreement. "On May, Vice-President Kostic proposed to President Izetbegovic that the talks be resumed with the participation of the representatives of the Bosnian, Serb and Croat communities. On the same day, authorities of the so-called Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina announced their decision to form their own army which will be composed of units of former JNA based in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and appointed General Ratko Mladic as the commander at that time." [Interpretation] So I assume that you know that as of that date, which was the 13th of May, 1992, that on that day, the authorities of the Republika Srpska proclaimed their decision to form their own army, which was not, as you know, under the command of Belgrade or under any kind of instructions from the JNA. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know this then, another thing that is written in this report to the UN Security Council. It is point 3, and it states as following: "On the 17th of May, I received a letter from Admiral Miroslav Simic [In English]: requesting assistance of JNA, requesting assistance in the safe withdrawal of JNA troops from Bosnia-Herzegovina and particularly from Sarajevo, Pazaric and Zenica. The letter referred, inter alia, to an agreement signed on May 1992 at the premises of the United Nations Protection Forces in Yugoslavia at Sarajevo by representatives of Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, JNA, the European Community Monitoring Mission and the personal envoy of Lord Carrington, Mr. Leonard Doyle. On 21st May, Vice-President Kostic again wrote to ask me to request President Izetbegovic to order the deblocking of the JNA garrison at Sarajevo. On 25th of May, I received a letter from President Izetbegovic in which, inter alia, he requested that UNPROFOR should supervise the withdrawal of part of JNA personnel and weapons in accordance with agreement of 10th of May, 1992." [Interpretation] So all this was agreed. The JNA was under the -- in the process of withdrawal, and they massacred the JNA soldiers who were in fact withdrawing. And then in point 5, he goes on to say: "The bulk of the JNA --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have the opportunity of dealing with these matters. Mr. Kirudja, do you know anything about these matters which are being raised by the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the matters that -- he's reading information from the Security Council, documents that contains information that reaches the Secretary-General from other sources, multiple sources, inclusive areas to which I do not have direct information. One of those areas is in the context, the substance raised in the last paragraph about matters going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina between JNA commanders in Sarajevo and what happened in that incident that is referred to as a massacre. Earlier on, when I said directly to Mr. Milosevic I don't know, it was with regard to the substance of what I thought was in the report of the Secretary-General was a conclusion he was drawing from the report of the Secretary-General that -- the text has moved in front of me. I can't recover it again, earlier on, but it was a point on -- that I understood to be a conclusion he was drawing and to which I referred. I don't know the fact of that conclusion or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was just quoting the text. I wasn't making any conclusions or observations from it. But do you know about this, another thing it says in point 5: "The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens [In English] of that republic and were not therefore covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision on withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina." [Interpretation] I assume you also know about that, Mr. Kirudja, that the army of Republika Srpska was established.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified, Mr. Milosevic, to that -- to being informed about those soldiers of the JNA that were to withdraw and those which were to remain. I have testified to that, in effect that those who were considered born in the area would be leaving, and those who were outside the area would remain. That I have testified to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, did you have information of this kind, like the one that was published by the London Independent on the 22nd of August, it was a Saturday, 1992, written by Leonard Doyle of New York, a correspondent of theirs, and he speaks not only about the fact that the forces, the extremist forces under the command of Izetbegovic did what they did, what we've just been talking about, but other crimes against their own population. It says here as follows: "[In English] United Nations officials and senior Western military officers believe --" [Interpretation] I'll read slower. Yes. Thank you. "[In English] United Nations officials and senior Western military officers believe some of the worst recent killings in Sarajevo, including the massacre of at least 16 people in the bread queue were carried out by the city's mainly Muslim defenders, not Serb besiegers, as a propaganda employ to win war sympathy and military intervention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness has given no evidence about Sarajevo, was not based there, so is not in a position, I would think, to deal with it. But, Mr. Groome, perhaps you can help me with this: Are you intending to call witnesses who will be covering Sarajevo in due course and who may be in a position to deal with these sort of allegations?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is the intention of the Prosecution at this stage to call witnesses to deal with Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Better put those to witnesses who know about Sarajevo. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue, but this is an essential point in view of the fact that Mr. Kirudja was a high-ranking UN official.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says here: "[In English] The view has been expressed in confidential reports --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Kirudja, you're being asked about a report from a correspondent dealing with events in Sarajevo and comments which are said to have been made by a United Nations official in relation to events there. As you've heard, it is the intention of the Prosecution to call witnesses to deal with Sarajevo, but since you're giving evidence, it may be right to ask you. Can you give any evidence about what happened in Sarajevo or in the bread queue or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I certainly couldn't speak even to the question of the journalist's stated report of which I don't have a copy or direct knowledge. I can't testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you can put that to a witness who can deal with it, but there's no point putting it to this witness. He knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm not going to put questions about it. But this is an essential point, Mr. May, because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. information and facts and figures about that were confidential. They were not made public. And the massacre perpetrated by the Muslim forces were taken as a pretext for introducing sanctions, because this was ascribed, this act was ascribed to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the way in which we waste time, your limited time in cross-examining, arguing about matters with which a witness cannot deal. Now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back, then, to your own territory. I have here a document which is entitled the UN Security Council Report Pursuant to 721 UN Security Council Resolution. It is general distribution. The date is the 4th of February, 1992. Point 4 speaks about the talks that Goulding had, both in Belgrade and in Zagreb, and so on and so forth, in Knin, and in all three areas under UN protection where it says that meetings with the leaders of the Serb community, under the protection of the UN, the Serb leadership asked that Mr. Goulding give further explanations to local leaders with respect to the UN peace forces' plan and react to the concern expressed by them with respect to that plan. Do you happen to remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have readily a copy of that, but both the names, Mr. Goulding is somebody I know about, his presence or visit in the areas we were deployed, I would have some understanding of that. So if you are specific about it, we can -- I can perhaps comment. But I don't have in front of me the report you are referring to. If you get specific on it, we can -- I may perhaps be able to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this report, it also says the following, that the deblocking was implemented -- this is point 6A, the cease-fire chapter or paragraph, and the deblockade was effected and the JNA units withdrew from Croatia and a satisfactory advancement was reached with regard to the humanitarian aspects, and so on and so forth. Then it is emphasised that the deployment of forces does not mean a change in the status quo and any arrangements with respect to the police would be pursuant to point 19 of the plan, and from this, it emerges that the area under UN protection, as has been the case up till now, would not come under the laws and institutions of the Republic of Croatia in the transitional period until a political solution is found. Is that so or not, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, it is. We have discussed the detail of this when we were talking about the Vance Plan, and this is another confirmation of what the Vance Plan required. But you have read the part that required the Croats not to have an influence during the transition period. The Vance Plan also required the Serbs not to institute any new structure in the area, yes. That is part of what we have testified to and discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now that we're discussing this issue, the recognition, the premature recognition both of Croatia and Bosnia and how it affected the deterioration of the situation, from that same report we can see that in Zagreb on the 28th of January, that's when Goulding went there to tour all the -- those who were on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, when he went to see Tudjman, that they could not accept the fundamental aspects of the plan by which they underline the unconditional acceptance of the plan expressed by my personal envoy and when it was stressed that the UN forces were deployed in the transitional period until a political solution is found or, rather, until political negotiations take place for a general solution, Mr. Tudjman said the following: After international recognition of his republic, there were no outstanding political issues to be discussed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't party to the meeting. This is obviously something Mr. Goulding himself was discussing, and if it is quoted in the UN report, I take it that it reflects what he was discussing with Mr. Tudjman. I wouldn't personally be testifying to its substance as it's obvious it was a meeting I wasn't participating in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can quote from this report, but then you must hand it to the witness so that he can read it. He must have the chance of dealing with it fairly, and merely to answer selective quotations from it is not a fair way of dealing with it. Now, is there anything more you want to ask him about it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Unfortunately, I only have these reports in Serbian, so there's no point in me showing it to the witness. But I gave you their numbers, the dates. I said that they were the UN Secretary-General's reports of those dates and that the distribution of the reports was general, general distribution, that's what it came under.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecution can help with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution will seek to obtain those reports, but if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Milosevic read, I believe in English, from the reports, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The earlier one. I don't know about this one. Yes. Do you want these reports exhibited, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall look for them in the original in English and then I will tender them. I will highlight the portions that I consider to be important and to which I wish to hear Mr. Kirudja's responses to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kirudja, in the report of the UN Secretary-General of the 28th of September, 1992, which speaks at the very beginning under chapter 1, violations of the truce or cease-fire, that tensions were big in the -- in Sector North, Miljevci, Peruca and so on, where the Croatian army stormed the area on the 21st of June, 1992. Do you happen to remember that? So these are violations of the agreement that I'm talking about, and the storming of the territory under UN protection by the Croatian forces. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one instance where the reference to giving me the report and the section would be certainly very helpful. Yes, there were instances of violation by both the Serbs and the Croats. I take it that that report, you're highlighting the part where the Croatian army was also reported to be in violation of the terms of the deployment of the nation in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this pertains to the Croatian violations of the cease-fire agreement. There is no mention of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why -- sorry to interrupt you. That's why I couldn't comment on the entirety of that report because I would have wanted to comment on whether it was just limited to a time period where it will focus one subject, or what it was. Right now, I have no way of understanding the -- what the nature of the report took, what the report intended to convey to the Security Council in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it precisely relates to violations of the Vance Plan and the aggression of the Croat forces against UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness is entitled to see is what the whole report says. All that we are getting from it is quotations, and it's not satisfactory that the witness cannot deal with it. Now, in future, you should produce these in English, if you have them, so the witness can deal with them. Mr. Kirudja, we will get these documents in due course. We will have the opportunity of reading the full reports, and we will allow the Prosecution, when they are exhibited, to draw our attention to other matters which the accused has not referred to. Since he's not able to put them, as he should have done, before you in English, that opportunity should be available. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree, Mr. Kirudja, in view of the fact that you have been referring to the Vance Plan quite specifically, and also recalling the UN Charter, any plan, including the Vance Plan, has to be in complete accordance with the UN Charter, and the general rules of conduct, including the rules that are in compliance with the plan, have to be in accordance with the UN Charter in general; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right, Mr. Milosevic, and you didn't even need to raise the point because the Vance Plan was ratified by a general -- a Security Council Resolution. And in order for the general -- for the Security Council Resolution to enable the mission, they would have taken care of the point you have raised. The Resolution, the enabling Resolution of the Security Council would have taken care of that point you are making.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the overall rules of conduct in the protected areas had to be interpreted in accordance with the UN Charter. So that is right, isn't it? I imagine that that is not being challenged in any way.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. As the representative of the United Nations, you certainly know that Article 2, paragraph 4 of the Charter refers to the prohibition of the use of force and threats of use of force and that there are two valid exceptions to that prohibition according to the UN Charter. One are collective military measures that are imposed with -- by the Security Council in accordance with Article 42 of the Charter, and the other one is self-defence envisaged in Article 51 of the Charter. Is that right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would like to ensure that you understand that the various parts of the Charter, it's not something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop, Mr. Kirudja. Stop, Mr. Kirudja. Please stop. Those are not matters for the witness. Those are legal issues on which the Chamber will have to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Robinson, but this has to do with the fact that I referred to yesterday, namely that it is precisely because of these attacks, totally unprovoked, against the UNPAs, the Serbs in that area used this inalienable right of theirs that is envisaged by the UN Charter as well, namely the right to self-defence, because, according to Article 51 of the UN Charter, one is allowed to defend oneself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll hear about this in due course and you can address us on it, on all these matters of law, but at the moment, the witness is giving evidence. You should concentrate on asking him questions, relevant questions at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kirudja, I presume that you agree that the Vance Plan and the Resolution of the UN establishing UNPROFOR did not refer to a situation whereby the population in UNPAs would have to be compelled to defend themselves. It was taken as a point of departure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us ask the witness. Your question, as so often, contains an assumption, which it should not. And the witness can help us about it. He may be able to assist us as to what the answer is. What is alleged is that the citizens, the population, as it's put, in the UNPAs had to defend themselves. Was that a situation that you saw on the ground when you were there, or not, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. The Vance Plan was designed to avoid that very issue, to avoid in the sense that the source of what would be a problem for the citizens was the armed units that were required to demobilise and have their weapons taken away in storage points, and then the United Nations, in their presence with the military and civil police, will monitor that there will be no return of such sources of threat and law and order would be kept by the own civilian police of the -- from the population, armed sufficiently for law and order and nothing more than that. So there wouldn't have been a reason for claiming that the population needed to defend itself under the terms of the Vance Plan and deployment of the UN assets in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kirudja. But when it became evident that UNPROFOR did not carry out its task and did not stop Croat attacks against UNPAs, namely when there was a situation that was not envisaged by the Resolution, do you agree that the Serbs rightfully resorted to self-defence as envisaged by Article 51 of the UN Charter? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about Article 51. And whether anyone was acting in self-defence may be a matter of law. But perhaps it can be put to the witness in this way: Did it appear to you that the Serb population, no doubt in reclaiming the arms of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Serb authorities, were acting in self-defence? Was this a situation, as it appeared to you, in which it was necessary for them or appeared necessary for them to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The circumstances leading to the first time and the last time those weapons were taken out of UN-controlled areas and subsequently were never returned to that, was an incident taken -- taking place in January somewhere in Maslenica. Again, I mentioned yesterday the distance of where that action was taken and the circumstances did not, in my view, justify the kind of repudiation of the status quo. It may have only caused a temporary concern to the local population which, I believe, the United Nations deployed mission was capable of addressing and dealing with in the traditional way we have dealt with matters of restoring the breach of the status quo. We never had a chance even to start repairing that breach. And there is every reason to believe that it was repairable, that breach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course it was repairable. But the breach was committed by the forces that attacked the UN protected areas. Can we, therefore, establish, Mr. Kirudja, that when force was resorted to by the Croat forces, in contravention of the Vance Plan and the UN Resolutions, the Serbs responded, acting in self-defence, which is an inalienable right. Can we say that it is the Croat forces that attacked unlawfully and that the Serbs protected themselves lawfully in accordance with the UN Charter? Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have put that question a number of times, and this is the last time that the witness will be required to answer it, if he feels he can add anything to what's already said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would rather take the counsel of the court that as to whether or not they had a self-defence was a matter of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a matter of law. You're absolutely right about it. Perhaps you can help us to this extent: First of all, do you agree with the accused's suggestion that it was the Croats, as it were, who started it, putting it in very simple terms, by being in breach of the agreement and attacking in the -- or making attacks in the protected zones? Is that general picture right or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, it is. And one report, and I had written in December, just weeks before that attack had occurred, I recall myself telling my headquarters this was going to happen. It's not anywhere in evidence here. It was a situational report that I had put out. I only missed by days when the Croats would take that action. I had even forewarned it. General Nambiar called me about it, and said, "Let's hope you're wrong." Unfortunately, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you -- could you clarify this for me. It has just gone off the screen, but I noted what you said earlier, that the distance in relation to where they -- and I'm paraphrasing -- where the action was taken did not justify the kind of repudiation of the status quo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, there were three distinct -- four distinct sectors where UNPROFOR was deployed. The further most from Maslenica was Sector East, close to the border with Serbia, in what is called now Eastern Slavonia. There was Sector West, which is somewhere in the middle as you come from Belgrade, and then Sector North of which I drew the approximate boundary, bordering on Western Bosnia, the Bihac pocket; and then Sector South, which spread all the way to Zadar and parts of Peruca down that you heard referred to, and then Maslenica Bridge an isthmus connecting the Dalmatia north and south. When the Croats took action in this very small, relatively speaking to the areas deployed, the Serbs took weapons from everywhere, including Sector East. Everywhere. They came out from everywhere almost simultaneously. That's why I mentioned that had it been otherwise, where the Serbs would have lodged a complaint to UNPROFOR and United Nations, this is a violation by Croatia in this particular point, the normal process of repairing that breach is what I'm referring would, in my opinion, have been possible. As it turned out, it wasn't, and the weapons never went back, despite our best efforts to restore that Vance Plan requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was a mechanism for violations to be lodged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And not only violations to be lodged, restoration of the breaches between the warring parties. That's what military component of UNPROFOR was all about, trying to repair that. In fact, I may even turn it the other way around: We had many from the Serb side across Bosnia in big ways, but the Bosnian Muslim forces that were deployed in the Bihac pocket specifically - the 5th Corps commanded there - did not do what the Serbs did, for example, come massively. They lodged a complaint that this was a violation, and we worked months to restore the breach and were successful in doing it. Therefore, there was a mechanism for repairing such breaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. May I proceed? I hope that you are going to discount this portion of my time that you are using for your own conferrals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, when aggression is carried out against a particular territory, what about the rest of that territory? Nobody is supposed to care at all; right? So the level of excitement has to be matched exactly to that part of the territory where the aggression took place, and the others should sleep peacefully, although the preconditions set forth in this plan is that peace would be guaranteed. So what guaranteed to the Serbs that there would be no further incursions once the plan was violated? What you said just now, does that seem logical to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what I said certainly does seem logical to me in terms of my explanation. I didn't understand your question, though. Please rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that you explained that this was an attack of the Croat forces against the Maslenica Bridge. I also mentioned the attack, the aggression on the Miljevice plateau, and then Western Slavonia, and then yet again your sector when hundreds of thousands were ethnically cleansed, and so on and so forth. So these fears on the basis of which the Serbs defended themselves, didn't they prove to be justified, that this was not some kind of isolated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not following the question. It's not at all clear. What the witness has said is that the removal of the weapons was not justified in the particular circumstances. Now, you seem to be putting something about later events, as far as I can see, and I don't really see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Relevance seems to be a very popular word here, but let's move on because I'm sure that you will drastically restrain my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the impression that we were not in agreement as concerns the implementation of the plan as it was written. Here's a Resolution of the Security Council, 762/92, on the 27th of July, 1992, related to a report of the Secretary-General, and it meant what UNPROFOR was doing. Then point 4 says: "Another important achievement was the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army (the JNA) from all sectors mentioned in the plan with the exception of one infantry battalion in Sector East that will be withdrawn within the next few days." That's what it says here in the report of the Secretary-General. So I have quoted a report to you, a specific one with a specific date so you can have a look at it, so can we agree, then, that the Yugoslav side fully complied with the plan, carried out its obligations based on the plan?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I did testify that yes, the JNA did withdraw for the period you have mentioned. The report was in July; correct? I believe it is. And that period of time there was the withdrawal of the JNA in the manner I testified yesterday. But you are also saying that constituted a fully -- a full compliance with the Vance Plan. No, it couldn't. The Vance Plan did not accept -- or it was inconsistent, the events that followed. Once they mobilised the troops who were supposed to stay that way. Weapons withdrawal, they were supposed to stay that way. The numbers for police necessary for law and order, they were never compiled with. What the police for maintaining law and order, as envisaged or designed in the mission, that was never complied with. So it is not correct to say or to draw the conclusion on the basis of that report at that point in time, in July, that could, the Vance Plan was fully complied with. No, it wouldn't be correct to draw that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was whether Yugoslavia - so the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had been formed - and it withdrew the Yugoslav People's Army or, rather, what belonged to them. Did Yugoslavia fulfil its obligation or not? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Your question says "fulfil its obligation." My response has to do with withdrawal of the JNA from that area. I'm not sure the two equate to each other. While I can accept that they withdrew for the period of time in the manner described, I couldn't also conclude fully full obligations of Yugoslavia. I wouldn't want to go into that because the two are not the same in my reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This will have to be discussed with others as well. Of course including some that I quoted yesterday and others who took part in this as well. Mr. Kirudja, yesterday you spoke about the focus of your activities being on cooperation with the local authorities in the sector that you were in charge of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cooperation with the local authorities? Rather, the local authorities were to cooperate with us to fulfil the mandate, and we in turn work with then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This morning -- since people are watching this on television very carefully in Yugoslavia, this morning I got a letter or, rather, a statement of Mile Bosnic, president of the municipality of Slunj. So this is a person who in the period from 1991 to 1993 was president of the municipality of Slunj. Mile Bosnic. This is a person that you communicated with. Your communications focused on the presidents of municipalities, as you said to me yesterday, and you considered that to be your task. I would like to ask you to comment on the following. I am not going to read the entire letter because it will take up too much of my time but I would like you to comment on some of things that this letter says, and I'm going to give it to you anyway. This is the way he starts: "It is interesting that all the killings of the Serbs in Slunj were something that you doubted. You wondered who the perpetrators were because you did nothing to have evidence. In Jelov Klanac, five persons were killed, et cetera. People were killed when they went hunting, Gojko Rakinic, and they were imprisoned in Karlovac. Serbs were probably killing themselves, and they probably took themselves to prison in Karlovac. We asked you many times to prevent this because this was your responsibility, and you kept refusing that, and you kept asking for some kind of evidence. When a man were even kidnapped, that was no proof for you. And when 600 persons were prevented from reaching Velika Kladusa, although they were armed, 70 managed to get through and so on and so forth, and they were led by members of the Croat army who originally came from Slunj."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. The witness should have the chance of dealing with these allegations which your correspondent makes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Point number 1, yes, I was aware of and I testified yesterday and in my testimony there are references to meetings in Slunj with a mayor. My notes say Bosic. Probably I missed the 'N', Bosnic as mentioned by Mr. Milosevic today. He met with me many times, and we dealt with a wide range of subjects, including humanitarian affairs, claims of refugees, and other matters. The statement I see in front of me, I can only react to it as wild. It looks wild to me. I can't recognise any of these matters. Neither can he say when and where he raised these matters with me. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I would rather want him to substantiate these things rather than me respond to them, because I have no recollection of the matters he is raising me refusing to hear or even listen. My testimony includes the issue of the five Croats that came in the municipality of Slunj, which were themselves, these Croats, removed from the south of Slunj in the area of Korenica, which he agreed, if he is the same person that is the mayor that was reported to have met with me, he agreed with his police chief, Mr. Klipa, to protect these people. So my memory of him was rather a memory of a person who wanted to do what was right. He wouldn't have -- I wouldn't have reached an agreement with him about protecting Croats at the expense of the municipality of Slunj. When I was being characterised as the statement being read by Mr. Milosevic, if it were true, he would not have reached a deal with me then. More specifically, I knew he was worried about that deal because of Mr. Martic. That is a reason I wrote a letter conveyed to Mr. Martic that these people needed protection as a way of allaying the fear of this man so he can do his job, so he can execute his responsibilities. And he did to our satisfaction. It couldn't be the same kind of person now issuing the kind of statement Mr. Milosevic read, which appeared to me wildly exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The letter is signed. I'll let you have it. I received it by fax, so this isn't an original, but you can read it through in its entirety, and I'm sure you'll recall this, he says at the end: "Do you remember who first came to your assistance when you and your associates had a traffic accident in Vosnjica? We didn't pass by and leave you there. It was Mile Bosnic with his associates." And underneath, we have the signature of Mile Bosnic himself. I'm sure you remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember an incident of that kind. Parenthesis: I recall yesterday mentioning there were so many speeches given to us by people like mayors of areas like Vojnic and others, and I characterised those speeches as very political, including why we can't live together with known Serbs, why we in the United Nations had to understand this if there was going to be peace. This is in the direction of so many of those wild speeches we had to listen to. So this particular -- I also recall a lot of accusations made that we couldn't verify even in our best tries. This is an example of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll hand you the letter. And he also says: "Do you know --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, you won't. It's simply a letter sent to you. It's of no probative value, and it's quite unnecessary for the witness to look at it. If you want to put anything else from it you can, but otherwise it is of no relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This isn't a letter sent to me. It is a statement concerning the testimony of Charles Kirudja before The Hague Tribunal which I received by fax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you fail to produce the important documents, namely the UN Security Council and Secretary-General ones. Those were admissible, but you failed to produce them. This is totally irrelevant and is totally inadmissible, so the witness simply won't see it. Now, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite the reverse, Mr. May. I said that I will be giving them to you in English because I have them in Serbian, and I just quoted one which was in English, that is true. And I said that I would like to have them tendered into evidence and that I shall let you have them in due course and that you can compare my quotations with the portions of the statement to see whether I have quoted them correctly or whether I've erroneously interpreted them. I think that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, never mind. I don't want to go on quoting Bosnic, but is what he says true, that the Serbs in Kordun received 50.000 to 60.000 refugees from Bosanska Krajina at that period of time? Is that true? People who had fled from Bosnia and Krajina. Do you know about that, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my testimony a little earlier did cast doubt whether the same person claiming to be mayor of Slunj is some fact I cannot even testify to. Given those wild accusations, I'm not even sure who it is that is making that allegation and whether he's really the person that he says to be. I have no way of doing that. Consequently, I'm unable to respond to information that you passed to me from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the fact here now, Mr. Kirudja. Do you know about the number of refugees who fled to Kordun from Bosanska Krajina? Serbs I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs who came into the Sector North from Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From Bosanska Krajina, that is to say from the whole Bosanska Krajina region, not just Krupa. Krupa is one municipality, but from the whole area of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demarcation of that Bosanska Krajina, would that encompass Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc, the areas I referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the ones you said bordered on your sector from which the Serbs fled under pressure and terror perpetrated against them by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This is a point that I did not testify directly. The presence of many Serbs in Sector North that had come from that area that we just described. There were cases that I got to know, but importantly, they were never represented to us as refugees. They came there without duress, apparently, settled in many of the evacuated houses that were in the sector, and consequently, they were never raised to us on the Serb side. On the contrary, I had long meetings from the Croatian side, complaining about that, that there were these aliens or, rather, they were considered to be people who had settled in the sector that were not supposed to be there. So the point you made, Mr. Milosevic, would have only come to my attention and our attention from the Croatian side as a complaint, not from the Serb side as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that that year, for example, there were already 100.000 persons from Croatia who were refugees in Serbia, let alone the other parts. Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's a different question from the one you asked me earlier. In Serbia or in the sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying is that from Croatia, already at that time, at the beginning of 1991, there were 100.000 refugees in Serbia, Serbs from Croatia who had fled under duress, under the pressure of killings, their houses being burnt and mined, et cetera. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, in 1991 we hadn't deployed there, and when we arrived, we only heard summaries of people being displaced and being located all over the former Yugoslavia, specifically in Serbia because -- and a lot on the Croatian side of that confrontation on the sector. Yes, we had some reports of displaced people in various locations, but I couldn't testify to the exact numbers prior to the arrival of the mission or even thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even thereafter, yes. Right. Now, I'm taking care of the pages. And on page 26, paragraph 4 of your statement, you say the following: "On the 15th of July, at 11.00 in Sisak, I had a meeting with Mr. Ramljak and the mayor of Sisak. The mayor said that in the Sisak area, there were already 15.000 to 20.000 refugees or displaced persons, and recent arrivals of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina were putting further pressure on the local authorities. He stated that 10.000 Serbs had left Croatia for areas controlled by the Serb authorities and that the fate of 1.500 Croats left behind in the UNPA area are still -- was still unknown." That's how you reported from the meeting, and I'm quoting this from your own statement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. What I want to ask you is the following: I assume that you consider yourself to be objective, so when you speak about the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, when you speak about the Muslim inhabitants who were fleeing from the war, you're talking about the displaced persons and persecuted persons and ethnic cleansing. But when you speak about the Serbs who under the most brutal of circumstances were expelled from Croatia, you use the term "they left." You say they left, as if it was a case of just somebody simply moving from one area to another, in this case the Serbs. So do you distinguish, therefore, on ethnic grounds when you're talking about refugees, that some went under pressure and some were the victims of ethnic cleansing whereas others just happened to go, just like that? So they're different verbs that you're using there. You're using the verb to cleanse and the verb to leave. Why do you reserve for the former category the verb to cleanse and for the latter category the verb to leave? Could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. First, it's a misreading of my testimony that you have. Clearly, that part of the testimony is reporting what the Croats were -- a representation made to me by the Croats in that meeting that you referred to. This sentence you read is not me saying. It says, "He stated." Somebody else stated that. Therefore, reflection of what I heard from the meeting, not characterising it one way or the other. I'm aware of the sensitivity of the -- from the Serbian side, that their refugees, their victims are understated. That perception that you alluded to in your question. But, sir, you mislead me very, very seriously when you attribute the wording of cleansing and others as me selectively using those words. I invite you to look at that text as you're given to in a more exacting manner. I take it you are referring to when we were discussing about testimony in Bosanski Novi of representations made to me on the one side and our own assessment of the effect of moving 4.000 people that turned out to be 9.000. That was not reported speech, that was direct assessment of an issue we were involved in. What you read today is just a reference to a story given to me and given back and reported exactly the way it was heard. I believe the language clearly makes that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The way it was heard. All right. But on page 28, paragraph 4 -- page 28, paragraph 4, you say that: "Regardless of whether we had a mandate for that or not, we have the moral responsibility of having the world hear the story told to us by numerous people who are fleeing from this part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was right across, immediately opposite our post." This is the Croatian translation of your statement, but that's what you said. So did you have any information as to how many Serbs were expelled from Croatia during your mandate there while you were there or around the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, again to illustrate the point I made earlier, on page 28, your reference to "our moral obligation," it's not in the context of reporting how Serbs were treated or not. That paragraph deals with an issue that was my own reaction to my headquarters telling us not to be involved "in what was going on across the border in Bosnia." It wasn't a reference to the Serbs or Muslims. Once again, it's a mischaracterisation of my testimony in that part. So I kindly ask you to look at it as carefully as we give it, because we were as sensitive, as you would know, to every side's feelings of victimisation and attempted to report it as accurately as we could, including distinguishing when we are telling a story as we heard it or telling a story as we observed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. If we may, let's make rational use of our time. I understand you when you say that there is a moral obligation to let the world hear the story, as I quoted from your statement a moment ago. So I assume that you had the feeling of this moral obligation to let world hear the story and about the tens of thousands of Serbs who were expelled from Croatia. And please, even The New York Times, in 1993, wrote about the figure of 10.000 mined Serb houses in Croatia and the enormous number of refugees, and so on and so forth. So it wasn't any Serb propaganda. That's not what it was about. And that Croatia was outside the UNPAs and that it was already ethnically cleansed before that. So were you aware of all those facts? I mean, why, intentionally or unintentionally, do you not deal with the exodus of the Serbs? And a priori, you seem to accept Ramljak's statement that quite simply they had left the area. So the one were expelled, and Ramljak says these people Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just left, and that's your area of responsibility, in your zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has already answered all this. He's already dealt with it, so let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but move on to another topic that we haven't covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 33 of your statement, paragraph 2, you talk about a coordination meeting held in Topusko on the 12th of August, 1992, which was attended by the UNHCR, International Red Cross Committee, the EMEZ, UNMO, Danbat - I assume the Danish battalion - and the representative of the UNHCR and Sector South, you discussed the problem of the 28.000 potential refugees from Bosnia which, via your area of responsibility, Sector North, wished to go to Croatia or, from Croatia, further on into Europe. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, did you happen to ask yourselves why these Muslim refugees from the northern parts of Bosnia did not wish to find refuge further into Muslim territory, which would have been more logical, would have stood to reason and would have been nearer, if the Serbs were actually trying to ethnically cleanse them, as you say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The more natural question is the one I asked, Mr. Milosevic: Why do people want to leave their own homes where they are secure if they're leaving voluntarily, not where they're going?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, taking this example, is it clear, using that example, that these people were fleeing from the war and from hunger and also from forcible mobilisation to which they were subjected by these extremist elements and the authorities of Izetbegovic? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony pointed when I asked the question I was given a different answer. It was by mayor -- the Mayor Pasic's own response, it was pressure brought to them by what he called Serbian irregulars. That's in response to my direct question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And was it precisely this radical fundamentalism and the absence of any kind of desire to live alongside the Serbs and Croats that later led to the inter-Muslim clashes, bloody ones in Cazinska Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. You haven't listened to the answer. The answer was that it was the Serb irregulars who drove them out, not the Muslims. So again, you simply take no notice of the evidence and just read on. Do you know anything about the inter-Muslim clashes, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only a specific one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can help with us that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was much later and in Bihac pocket, when Mr. Fikret Abdic decided to give rise to his Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia. The area that up to that point was controlled by one army, the 5th Corps of Bihac, split into two, and there was Muslims facing each other in that area, one side supporting Fikret Abdic and the other side loyal to the government in Sarajevo. That's the one inter-Muslim clash that I was thoroughly familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, do you know that Abdic received the largest number of votes at the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that his position as president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina he gave to Izetbegovic, saying that Izetbegovic was a politician and that he was a businessman and did not wish to be president. Do you know that he was one of the most popular men among the Muslims at that time and he won the largest number of votes. Is that something that you know about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Abdic himself did tell me a lot of what you've said and he delighted in reminding me and my colleagues about specifically having won the largest amount of votes in Bosnia, and specifically that he had a vision of how to solve the problem. So yes, directly from Mr. Abdic I did hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you spoke about the Belgrade declaration. Do you know that Abdic -- this whole territory of Western Bosnia proclaimed to be an autonomous province. That's what he did, and the main objective was peace, that's what he proclaimed, and good neighbourly relations with the Serbs and the Croats. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, I testified yesterday, that was the gist of his vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He came to see me. He informed me that he had been to see Tudjman as well and that what he wanted was to establish all kinds of relations - first of all, economic relations and all the other types, cultural, political ties - both with Serbia and with Croatia and with Republika Srpska and with Republika Srpska Krajina, and he asked for my support for this kind of peace-loving policy. Is that something you know about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified to that gist of the Belgrade declaration that Mr. Abdic presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was published in the papers. We welcomed it, welcomed the desire of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia along those lines, which was a purely Muslim one at the time, to live in peace, and this desire was also welcomed by the Republika Srpska Krajina and Republika Srpska and also by Croatia, as far as I was informed, both by Tudjman and Abdic. And normal economic relations were established. For example, we supplied him from Serbia with food for the production of livestock, for livestock rearing and the other manufactures he needed for the factory and Agrokomerc company. So we sent him assistance in this way, and we were very happy to see that this was taking place and that an area like that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was completely inhabited by Muslims who had professed their desire to live in peace with everybody. And they were able to move around freely across both borders. They would go to Zagreb and to Belgrade alike, and they could travel around in Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina. Do you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long statement, Mr. Milosevic. I did know that Mr. Abdic had that capacity. He freely moved his assets, including trucks, as -- between his Bihac pocket, the Krajina, and Croatia, and Zagreb and Karlovac, all the way to Rijeka. I was aware of all of that. And he did it actually without any assistance or need for assistance from us when he was dealing with the part where we are at. He was able to arrange it all by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know what kind of massacre Izetbegovic's forces from Bihac, that 5th Corps, effected against Muslims, exert -- Muslims who adopted for peace and support to the policy of peace as led by Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I had the opportunity of dealing directly with that command of BH 5th Corps in the context of the Serbs' army in the Sector North forcefully crossing the international border and taking a huge chunk of the area that international -- that was across the international border, starting with the first area where the Serbs made an incursion, Blinski Kut [phoen], and then a much bigger incursion in an area Bosanska Bojna. During that, because the incursion had taken place from Sector North and because of the instability that it caused, there was a threat of retaliation from the 5th Corps into the sector. During that course, I did meet with the commander of that 5th Corps, Rasim Dreskovic, many, many times with the sector commander. In the course of that period of meetings on both sides, I did hear a lot of claims of atrocities. They were not one-sided. They came from both sides as a result of the -- that attack that came in. So I couldn't tell you how many numbers were involved, but there certainly were casualties as a result. But the -- it became a three-way fight, complicated, because Mr. Abdic enlisted the military support of both the forces of the Serbs located in operational zone Kordun and operational zone Banija. In essence, he would get them to do their heavy fighting without getting the weapons. He would get their active support. Then big 5th Corps command, which was loyal to Sarajevo, then that command began to fight both the splinter part headed by Mr. Abdic, located in the area of Velika Kladusa, and it fought both that part and the Serbs. Therefore, in that context, the claim that there were massacres has to be understood in that three-way -- three-way conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. May, may I have more time for the cross-examination of this witness, or are you going to insist that I conclude my cross-examination now before the break? Because I have quite a number of questions to ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. When we get back, you will have ten minutes more, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, ten. You've had plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two matters. I have a copy here of a reference book from the library, Yugoslavia Through Documents. It's an English copy of, I think, most of the UN documents. I will make it available to Mr. Milosevic during the break. Any pages that he wishes to seeks to introduce, I will have them photocopied after I receive it back, if that's acceptable to the Court. But this should include the documents that he had in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He may find it difficult, quite honestly, in 20 minutes to do that. I wonder if the Court could have that document, that book, and make the photocopies. Anyway, let us consider it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just one matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing before we move on. I don't want to lose this. It's important that we get the documents now and we know what documents they are. Yes. We'll consider it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just one matter in the interests of saving time. I would ask Mr. Kirudja, over the break, to review his notes of the 5th of May and the 27th of May. I will be asking him a couple of questions regarding those two meetings. That's the 5th and 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, in your letter which was provided here under tab 11, you said certain things which are not correct. So I would like to challenge that. You say, "Following the secret meeting --" First of all, there was no secret meeting. The FRY-BiH border, we never met at a border. [In English] border was allegedly closed for all males from RS aged from 18 to 65 without the special permission from RS military Rade Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness have the document first. It's tab 11 of this exhibit binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you say: "His" - meaning my - "relationship with General Mladic by cutting off the rate of desertion from the BSA." Do you know that this very painful measure that we took, namely, the blockade of the border towards Republika Srpska, was taken in 1993, after the Assembly of Republika Srpska refused to accept the Vance-Owen Plan that Karadzic had signed in Athens, however, the Assembly in Pale refused it, in spite the efforts made by myself and the then president of the FRY Cosic and Greek Prime Minister Mitsotakis. So this was a painful measure of pressure upon the leadership of Republika Srpska to accept the Vance-Owen Plan and it had nothing to do whatsoever with the age group of men from the ages of 18 to 60. It meant a total blockade. After that, even the European Union asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're supposed to be asking questions. It's simpler if it's done one by one. Just a moment. Let the witness deal with it. The first point is it was a measure to put pressure upon the leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the document that is in front of me is dated May 1995. I could mention that I did report on the painful decision Mr. Milosevic referred to, though I didn't characterise it as painful. I did characterise that it resulted into strained relationship with those who opposed that decision, specifically Karadzic and others. I did report separately of the painful decision that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you didn't call it that, but it was painful for us. But is it undeniable that this measure was introduced in 1993, not in 1995? It has nothing to do with 1995. And this is the first time that I hear that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mladic had some problems with desertion. Problems of desertion in the army of Republika Srpska, even if they did exist, were marginal. I had never heard of them. How did you come up with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, my role was to coordinate all the sources of information from the military observers, from our civil affairs, from the other information reaching us and piece together what they meant. So this -- these reports, these and other reports that have been put there are a reflection of multiple sources that were reaching our force -- our offices. I draw your attention that it is also carefully worded to say allegedly, because we couldn't verify all pieces of information. The word "alleged" or "reportedly" is peppered around this where we couldn't completely verify the information. Thirdly, I'd like the record to be understood when these reports were done was for different purposes than they are being used today. They were not intended to be court documents or others. This was supposed to alert, forewarn in the direction so we would restrict them because we couldn't verify everything. So this was restricted information intended for different purposes, not in the strict evidentiary rules that you would want to apply to them now. That was the purpose with which they were being written. Those who were the sources, collective sources of the UN that we put together in our sit room, in our briefings, and putting together and drawing conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You draw the wrong conclusion, because you should know that even the European Union asked to place a monitoring mission at the border, and we agreed with that because we had nothing to hide. This mission was headed by Bo Pellnas, a Swedish general. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pellnas and I are well-known and we frequently -- he was one of the people where we would cross-check information reaching us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Pellnas report to you about anything that had to do with any kind of violations that his mission established as concerns that blockade?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no reporting role to me. We were just collocated and parallel responsibilities, but knowing each other from our UNPROFOR engagement, we had a very cordial relationship, so I did get the benefit of his advice and insight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you, although there was no subordination between the two of you, there was coordination, rather, did he ever tell you that there were problems and that the regimen that we had established was being violated in any way? Did he ever say that to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I was able to say with regard to that would be what is on record itself, what I have said and what has been shown on the record. If you're referring to any specific part of what I have said coming from -- information coming from the monitoring mission that was shared between Bo Pellnas's office and mine, whatever I discerned from that, that's what I knew and that's what is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could not draw these conclusions then from his formulations. You had to draw these conclusions then from some other information, because we never got any objections from him with regard to that particular regimen. All right. Can we move on now? I have another question or, rather, I have a few more questions, but let's clarify one thing: You mentioned the freeing of hostages, several hundred members of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many efforts we made, political efforts, media efforts, all other kinds of efforts, in order to have these hostages released and to have each and every one of them returned to their families so that no families would be in mourning because of everything that had happened there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I was well aware of your effort, as conveyed to me very clearly by Mr. Stanisic, and I reported at length of the importance you placed on the safe release of these hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I have the impression, Mr. Kirudja - I don't know if you will agree with that - that the other side tried to abuse even this enormous effort we made to have these people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. That's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. They put a question to you: Did Stanisic have forces in Bosnia? And you said that he had forces in Bosnia. Stanisic had no forces in Bosnia. Do you know that or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question to me was some remark he had made and how I interpreted it. It was in the context of Stanisic requesting certain information from UNPROFOR so that he could use it through his contacts in Bosnia to do just what you said, secure the safe release of those hostages. The question put to me was was it my understanding that he was taking forces with me in the announced journey that he was going inside Bosnia to do -- to help in that release. My response yesterday was it was my understanding he was going to meet them there already. That's how I characterised it. Not that he had forces, not in the characterisation you made. I made that it was my understanding he was going to meet already on location operatives loyal to him to secure those hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. You know full well that these hostages were scattered all around -- all over Republika Srpska. If you can call that forces, Stanisic had only a few bodyguards of his own, his personal security, and also ways and means of establishing where the hostages were. In some places there were ten of them, in others 15, et cetera, but we did manage to establish that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time here. The witness has answered your question in what -- by explaining and clarifying what he meant. Now, your time is now up, but you can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I have a few more questions. I'll be very rational with my time. Is it clear to you that this was not a military or police operation? This was a political move done by political means and under great media pressure to have your hostages released and that actually everything that was done was done in a peaceful way, without any kind of fighting there or any kind of conflict, and they were all returned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I am aware that it ended up peacefully, and I was at Novi Sad when the last group of hostages were released unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more questions. Please, is it correct that the Muslim representative Muhad Safric [phoen] said to you that Muslims were leaving the area of the Bihac pocket primarily because of the poor economic situation, explaining to you extensively what he feared, and as you say, carefully trying not to accuse the Serbs? This is page 33.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that testimony, Mr. Milosevic. Indeed, that underlined he was very careful not to offend the Serbs in how he characterised the situation. Yes, it is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a representative of the UN, he did not have to be careful not to blame the Serbs in front of you if it was the Serbs who were really to be blamed for their leaving. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Kirudja?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I would draw a different conclusion for why he was careful. Even if he was in front of us, it was in a territory controlled by the Serbs, and he had to be careful not only for the moment he was in front of us but for the moment later when the meeting would end and be on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since we haven't got much time, I'm just going to deal with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You've got one more question. You're way over your time. You can ask one more.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting on the 13th of May, you were there, Neilson, General Bamaiyi. You were cautioned that there was information that the Croatian forces are going to conduct diversionary actions in the territory of the Republic of Krajina. Do you remember that and do you remember the protest that was lodged because of the liquidation of five civilians on the 15th of May at 1500 hours at Jelov Klanac by this same terrorist group consisting of Mile Gasparevic [phoen], Sabla Stijepan [phoen], Gracan Ivan, a certain Mladen, all of them from the village of Sabjetci [phoen], and on that occasion, the following persons were killed: Djordje Trbojevic, Ilija Trbojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
