utterances.text: We don't need a list read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was your mandate, Mr. Kirudja, your mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mentioned about allegations and certain casualties, and then you ask it was our mandate. I'm not sure what you meant it was our mandate with regard to what you prepositioned that with, the report that there were incidents. What mandate are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, can you help us at all, without going into that, about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question in what capacity he refers to our mandate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think it matters --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's making an allegation about the liquidation of five civilians on the 15th of May by some terrorist group. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to check my notes more carefully, because this was a repeated allegation from meeting to meeting. This specific meeting there could, but I need to check it carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would, please, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain this. When I say that this belongs to Mr. Kirudja's mandate, that means that these are crimes that were committed in a territory that was within the zone that was covered by Mr. Kirudja. That is the way in which I use the word "mandate."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what I was afraid of. I'm not even sure crimes were committed in our territory. You go to a meeting and you receive such-and-such happened, without investigation of where it happened and who caused it. It wouldn't be accurate to say it occurred in the sector where we were -- we had a mandate. It certainly wouldn't have been correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just put one more question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. We've really gone well over the time. Now, Mr. Tapuskovic, have you any questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have questions, and I'll try to be as efficient as possible. I'll really try to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kirudja, I'm just going to ask you about what you wrote down yourself, about what you testified about, nothing but that, of course in order to assist the Trial Chamber so that they could view matters as fully as possible. I would like to begin, if I can put it that way, from paragraph 2 on page 59 of your statement. It's the second paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the one about the flights?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You spoke about that, and I would like to remind you of what you stated to the investigators. Perhaps you can confirm this to me or explain what happened. This is what you said: "I surmised that the flights from the FRY to the RS were real and served as a warning by Yugoslav army generals to Milosevic that he could not and should not force the JA down a path with which they disagreed so strongly." And then you added: "Namely, many in the Yugoslav army were opposed to Milosevic's decision to close the border between the FRY and RS and his consideration of a possible recognition of Croatia and Bosnia in order to have sanctions against the FRY lifted. They viewed such steps as abandonment of the Serbs in the RSK and RS." Is that right? That's what you stated; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you then add what you established, namely: "Indeed, three days prior to the aforementioned flights into Srebrenica, 80 generals and colonels of the Yugoslav army publicly warned Milosevic that if he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. recognised Croatia and BiH, thereby disowning the RSK and the RS, they would disobey the Supreme Defence Council and the JNA commander and join the military forces of the RSK and RS." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to remind you of the statement that you made on the 26th of the -- of October, where De Mello was present, and you were there too. This is the meeting with Milosevic that you refer to on page 49, paragraph 2, of the English version. You stated there, and this is probably contained in your notes as well: "Milosevic also stated that problems in Croatia and the RSK could only be solved in Zagreb in a three-phase process involving a cease-fire, normalisation of day-to-day life, and political negotiations." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also added the following: "He also stated --" no, that's a bit further down. It's the last paragraph on that page. "No other approach would be good." That that is what Slobodan Milosevic said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Finally in relation to this subject, I would like to ask you about Jovica Stanisic. Before this procedure involving the refugee rescue operation, did you ever see Stanisic before that? Did you ever talk to him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until I met him for the purpose of that hostage release.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Stanisic in 1992, 1993, 1994 when you were carrying out your official duties on behalf of the United Nations in the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were very far removed from -- in 1992 and 1993, I was in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 14, paragraph 3, of the English version, in that statement of yours you refer to the meeting that you had on the 13th of May, 1992, with Paspalj.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 14.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that 13th of May, did Paspalj say to you, and he continually repeated that: "We don't have an army. The people are our army and cannot withdraw from here." This had to do with the demilitarisation of that zone. Is that what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that, did you also say to the investigators by way of your own conclusion: "Indeed, almost all men and some women between the ages of 16 and 55, and some who were younger and older than that, had a uniform and a weapon." Is that what you noted yourself, what you noticed yourself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the situation similar among the Muslims and the Croats? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to be more exact on that. Muslims and Croats in the sector where we were or across the border? Where did you want me to make that observation, that similar observation that I made about the Serbs? I understand did I notice it among the Muslims and Croats. Where would I notice that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you later, Mr. Kirudja, about borders, but I wonder about that area. Irrespective of borders, did you notice the same thing that you noticed in the case of the Serbs, that there were armed civilians and people in uniforms, or was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I sought clarification from you, it is where the Muslims and the Croats would be. For example, I didn't notice that among Croats I met in Zagreb or Karlovac. If you're not specific enough where the Croats you want me to comment are, it wouldn't be helpful. Similarly, I didn't notice that among the Muslims that I met at the early stages in Bihac and Velika Kladusa, for example, but -- so --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I'm interested in the following: This is what I would like to ask you: You did not witness the events that took place in 1991; is that right? You did not witness what happened all the way up to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course you cannot know what happened at that time. However, I would take the liberty of asking you the following: Can you say something about whether, at those points in time, there were some signs that there were conflicts akin to a civil war at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, plenty of them. When you arrive in that sector, there were burnt houses, unoccupied, mines, scenes of war, smoking tanks. The evidence of conflict was unmistakable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived in 1992, in the month of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Croatia, BiH, and Slovenia became members of the United Nations on the 22nd of May, 1992, at the plenary session of the General Assembly of the UN after you arrived? You came in April, and they were internationally recognised on the 22nd of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't doubt that date if you -- I myself didn't know the exact date, but fact that their flag was flying at the UN was unmistakable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, Mr. Kirudja, since until the 22nd of May there was not full international recognition of the newly created states, that at the moment when you arrived in the area, there were no internationally specified borders there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again your question carries a legal implication, "internationally recognised." I wouldn't be able to speak to that legal concept of internationally recognised. What I can say was that there were borders which were clearly observed and known, and that is the borders that corresponded to the republics that were constituent parts of the former Yugoslavia. That is like, in my sector, the border I traced on the southern side of the sector separating the sector from Bihac pocket. That was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, Mr. Kirudja, I wouldn't ask you this if on page 36, in paragraph 1, the last sentence -- could you please find that, actually.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Page 36, paragraph 1. The last sentence.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last sentence? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said there: "It was thus nothing more than a nominal international border." What did you mean by that when you said that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. A point I sought, again to explain my headquarters, that this -- although this was an internationally recognised border, and I meant the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Western Bosnia, Bihac pocket, and Sector North, that border, we, for operational purposes, divided it into two parts. The part where the population on the Bosnian side was predominantly Muslim, that is running right through Bihac, Velika Kladusa, and close to Bosanska Krupa or somewhere -- rather, Bosanska -- a little east of Velika Kladusa. That was truly a border where people were controlled. They couldn't freely cross from one side or the other. The Serb -- they would meet the Serbs if they're coming from Bosnia, and the Serbs will meet Muslims if they're coming from this sector. Beyond that, in the border separating the opstinas of Dvor and Kostajnica, that's the part I characterised as nominal border, meaning it was controlled on both sides by the Serb authorities and ordinary citizens who were Serbs freely crossed that border without reference to humanitarian crisis, people being arrested, all that. That's the meaning of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you, Mr. Kirudja, tell me this, please: The situation surrounding the borders, you know that at that time there weren't any borders of that kind for almost 80 years, and now suddenly these borders were being introduced. So the introduction of these borders at that particular point in time, was it of any significance with respect to the moving around of the population and that the establishment of those borders had perhaps triggered off the exodus of the population in certain directions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I just finished explaining the significance to us operationally. It was where ordinary people met resistance or hazard crossing the border depending on their ethnicity, and the borders I described just a few minutes ago, put strain on both Serbs and Croats if they wanted to cross that border within the limits I described. There were no such limits, there were no such stress, there was no such harassment if they were Serbs crossing in the other part of the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Could you now focus on what you said on page 30 of your statement, the last paragraph on page 30, in fact. In the middle of the paragraph, you state the following: "At the same time, the Serbs who wished to flee from the area of Cazin or -- known as the Bihac pocket, which was under the Muslim control, the border between the UNPA zone and Bosnia was considered to be theoretical." What I want to ask you is this: The Serbs, did they flee from the Bihac pocket? Did they leave the Bihac pocket?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I responded to that question yesterday or maybe today, this morning. I forget when. There were Serbs who had relocated from across the border into Sector North. Once again, I also mentioned if they had done so, it was with the full assistance or cooperation of the Serb authorities in the sector where they did not raise a request for assistance or protection by UNHCR, because once they arrived into the sector, they would be settled in one of the empty houses that were in the sector. So we wouldn't receive a lot of focus on those who were Serbs and were in this sector. And I explained this, I believe, in an attempt to say that we were not ignoring them. It is because they were not being raised, the issue was not being raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. A moment ago, you spoke about nominal borders. Were there conflicts -- whether there were conflicts in the various areas, you've already talked about that. Now, what I'm interested in is this: Did the conflicts break out in the locations which did not follow the nominal borders?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were conflicts, and I have -- I have described them where the Serbs were facing the 5th Corps of Bihac pocket. There were conflicts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Everything I've asked you so far I asked you because I wish to quote something that you yourself said from your notes and which is to be found on page 34 of your statement, paragraph 3. And in that paragraph, you speak of the following: There was a meeting at which the representatives of Serbs and Muslims and all the other communities living in the area took part, and the Muslim representative then added: "We fear reprisals each time Serbs are killed at the confrontation line. So far, the Serbian authorities have managed to prevent such reprisals. Today's movement should not be considered ethnic cleansing, it should be considered in the context of a life-threatening situation." That's what the Muslim representative said.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct, and that's what I reflected. I reflected that's what his representation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And did you also record the statement by another Muslim representative on page 35, paragraph 4, of your statement, and that particular Muslim representative from Bosanska Krupa said that he was disappointed with UNHCR's position. He claimed that applications for resettlement by many of those now wishing to leave had been submitted to UNHCR over a month ago. However, they had still not received a response from UNHCR. He stressed that 80 per cent of those wanting to leave had guarantees of accommodation and jobs elsewhere. He mentioned economic reasons, therefore. He said that winter was coming and people feared a worsening of conditions. That's what he said too.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then on the very next page, that is to say page 36 -- no, 37, paragraph 2, you speak about the time when the -- there was an incursion for ten or 15 kilometres into the Serbian Krajina region to protect the Serb population there; right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is page 36, second paragraph. Page 36, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You took note of this, and then after the negotiations: "Following negotiations conducted by the sector commander on both sides of the border, the Krajina TDF withdrew from this area and several hundred families arrived in the sector as refugees. They seem to have been resettled mostly in the Banija region of the sector." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, how many people this was and how -- how many people, actually, how many families?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good example of what I said earlier, that the Serbs would come with the assistance of the local people without a lot of fanfare and they would be settled and I wouldn't even know the numbers because they did not involve us. You're illustrating the point I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, yes. That's precisely why I'm asking you. So these several hundred families - I don't know how many people that actually was, because every family has a different number of family members - where did they go and what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering you by saying because of known involvement by the local authorities of us, we didn't have the details you seek.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you confirm here that several hundred families left, dislocated. So how many families? How many people, if you can tell us. If you can't, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then in continuation, you say: "Then, on the 24th of August, 1992, a military formation involving some 600 Muslims and Croats infiltrated the UNPA at Kamenica." What did that lead to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of those very troubling flashpoints where there was an attempt to cross over in the area of Plaski, by Muslims to the Croatian-controlled side of the sector. That paragraph continues to explain that the infiltration provoked serious political and military reactions among local authorities within the UNPA. It's a fairly destabilising incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, the 21st of September incident that you discuss on page 37 of your statement, paragraph 3, could we hear your comments? It was a conflict between Muslim and Serb elements erupted in the Bosnian villages of Poljana and Glinica, and then you state that tension grew and that it looked as if the Serbs were peacefully evacuated from the area and resettled in Prijedor. Do you know how many people those were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As tensions mounted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the incident I have elsewhere referred to as the Bosanska Bojna pocket. The same applies when Serbs moved their own people. They did so with their own means, and then we would only hear subsequently that so many people moved. We were not ourselves being asked to get involved. On the contrary, if the Croats were complaining about Croats in the sector, it is us who went to look for them because the Croatian authorities were not in a position to do so. And if there were Muslims in the sector, the same thing would apply. So you will see more details when other ethnic groups are involved and we are actively involved as opposed to when there are displaced Serbs and the Serbs were taking them to safety from one area to the other. It's a material distinction I come back to for -- to explain the absence of too many details about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I have to hurry up, so may I ask for shorter answers, please. I know that you need quite a lot of time sometimes, but could we have shorter answers now, please, to my next questions. A moment ago, you spoke about the movement of 10.000 Serbs after the meeting and talks with Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this: You, of course, tried to prevent the movement of the Muslim population, prevented people from leaving their homes, but in cases where there was this movement on the part of other ethnic groups, did you also hold joint meetings to prevent that from happening?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, precisely. I have said over and over again on that issue, it is reported to us that the Serbs were moved. We were not being asked to assist moving the Serbs. It's materially different from the other case you referred to where we are being asked to do so. In the case of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And just two more points that I wish to clarify, and both of them are contained on page 39, paragraph 4, of the English version of your statement, where you speak about an operation near Glina, and you say that at the end of that particular operation, five of the most wanted violent criminals were arrested and taken to a prison in Knin. "The local militia also verbally informed me that one person had been arrested in connection with the brutal murder of three Croats several months before. A written protest had been sent to the local authorities about the murders and the matter was raised periodically with the authorities." Is that correct? Was that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in 1993, you learnt, as you say a little lower down, about the terrible abuse perpetrated by the Croats in the Medak pocket. Did you write to the Croatian local authorities along those lines too? Did you write similar letters, asking them to find the perpetrators, the perpetrators of the crimes that you had -- your attention had been brought to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but the reason you don't see that Medak pocket in this story is because it was in Sector South, and all the communications and the UN action regarding Sector South were dealt with by somebody else. And to answer your question directly, the Medak operation did become a major concern by the Security Council on the action taken by the Croatians, but it won't appear in my testimony because it was in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, just one more point: With respect to evidence in tab 7, exhibits in tab 7, you spoke at length about that, and you used the term "concentration camp," and you compared that to what was going on -- what -- the events that took place in World War II; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe in a certain exchange when I was talking about my exchange with Nambiar, General Nambiar, about it, I did make reference to it, or some other context, yes, where he differed with the use of the word "concentration camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned this somewhere in your statement, but I don't have time to go back to that, but you used these terms about testifying to the locations here. You said, "we think," "we feel," "we are doing," "it seems," "allegedly," and so on, terms of that kind. Now, from your mission, your mandate, you didn't make any direct checks on site, on-site investigation and checking.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a generalisation that obviously my testimony would be contrary to. There are references in many places where we are definitive in what we say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: Did you ever deal in establishing such locations or, rather, people in a closed area? Did you go and see whether this was being done elsewhere, where Croats were being kept in prison or Serbs detained in places of that kind? Did you receive reports that things of that kind were going on elsewhere, and if so, did you go and investigate, check those reports out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again your question is broadly worded, and yes, there were incidents, depending on what incident you are talking about, where I myself was directly involved. I had been in prison in Glina, looking at people being held there. I was at the site of crimes when -- rather, in the site of where something happened. I was there. So your generalisation I don't understand. We were present in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All I'm interested in is this: Something that was established - concentration camps - on the basis of the reports of others, did you ever ascertain that there were similar camps where Croats and Muslims were being detained?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking this in the context of the list of the concentration camps I mentioned, and in that category, we just reported the information we were collecting from the people running away from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in none of these cases did you go on site anywhere in any case, whether it was a case of Muslims, Croats, or Serbs, to establish whether those places and locations where these people were kept, were being detained, had the features of concentration camps. Did you ever go to check it out and see whether the characteristics of these places were conducive to the term "concentration camp," that they could be characterised as being concentration camps, or did you just rely on the stories that were told and descriptions given?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is very broad. I'll answer it specifically only. In terms of those areas we were talking about, we didn't say we went there. We said there was a stream of people, well into hundreds, that were coming from there, and they sought safety first and then anonymity in what they were telling us, and we recorded the events they were describing. That's the extent I will go with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Mr. Kirudja be shown three -- Prosecution Exhibit 336, the map book, open to page 30 and 31. I'd ask that be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being down, Mr. Kirudja, there has been some discussion about Maslenica and where it is located. I'd ask you to look at what's being placed on the overhead. I've taken the liberty of placing a green tag there next to a village. Can you see the village there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to take the pointer. Is that the village of Maslenica --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- that you were referring to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this would be in the area of Split?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just south of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Milosevic put to you a number of Security Council reports and resolutions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw the map of Split here. That's in Central Dalmatia. That's not Maslenica at all. This is the island of Solta. It's got nothing to do with this. This is Split, Trogir, Central Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where should we be looking for the village that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bridge. The bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would have to go up north, if they want to look at the map. What's Split got to do with it? Just take a look at the map yourselves and you'll see for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... atlas with that name. Obviously, it's a matter we'll have to check out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And not being well versed with the geography of Croatia, I looked in the map index, and I invite everybody to look in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It appears --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- in the evidence too that it's dealing with somewhere else. No doubt we can get someone who knows about Croatia to deal with it. Mr. Kirudja, don't bother to look any more. We'll get somebody who knows the geography of the area to deal with Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One of the Resolutions that Mr. Milosevic put to you, or one of the reports, was dated the 28th of September, 1992. We now have copies of that report here in the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I note for the Chamber that we are in the process of locating the other reports and we should have them either later today or tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would ask that you take a look at this report that Mr. Milosevic asked you about, and he was referring you to the first chapter, the violations of the cease-fire. I would direct your attention to paragraph 4 of that report. It's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will exhibit this formally tomorrow, but let us have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to briefly review paragraph 4 on the second page and ask you whether that is a report of what you've referred to as the loophole, where special police essentially became a militia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This paragraph does succinctly capture the point we were making in the testimony. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it reported to the Security Council that the estimate of the size of this force was now 16.000 armed men?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in all the sectors combined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I would draw your attention now to paragraph 6 of this report, and I would ask you to simply read the first two sentences of that report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, on the next page.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR has increased its efforts to protect the known Serb populations from ethnic cleansing by the paramilitary units. As described in paragraphs 10 to 18 below, they engage in acts of terrorism against minorities, especially in Sector East and to a lesser extent in Sector South, and appear to enjoy complete impunity."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the course of Mr. Milosevic's cross-examination of you, he put to you a number of statements allegedly made by General Nambiar. At the time you made your observations about what was going on in Northern Bosnia, did General Nambiar have any UNPROFOR troops in those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. At the time you made your observations regarding the Northern Bosnian municipalities, was there an UNPROFOR presence in those Bosnian municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next question, if you can answer it yes or no should suffice: Mr. Milosevic suggested, or in a quote of General Nambiar, said the following: "Any genocide and killings or massacres on all sides that are typical of such conflict conditions." Yes or no if you can answer this question: Do you agree with that statement that killings and massacres were an inevitable result of the conflict conditions as you observed them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too difficult a question for me to answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many -- one of the reasons I say it was difficult was the -- there was a lot of reasons why both -- all sides exaggerated what they were telling us. So there was immediate difficulty at all times of verifying claims and counterclaims of existence of massacres, particularly those which were allegedly taking place before we arrived, and we were confronted with that reality time and time again and not being able to ascertain to ourselves where the facts lay in terms of who committed what massacres prior to our arrival. But during the present, when we were there in terms of the sectors themselves and within the sectors, if anyone alleged there was atrocities committed in a minority group, as Croats would allege that Croats in the sector were being subjected to that kind of pressure or misuse, we would ascertain for ourselves. We had the resources and the means to check. But not in Bosnia, on the other hand, where we were not deployed. But we were receiving, so to speak, the effect of the actions claimed to be happening, and that is a stream of human beings seeking refuge where we are and saying why they were leaving or trying to escape from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My final question to you is the following: Mr. Milosevic suggested to you that the situation in Bosnia deteriorated significantly upon the international community's recognition of Bosnia. You've testified here that the mass movement of Muslims into Sector North began, and you received this information from your discussions with Serb mayors, that this mass exodus began when these Muslims refused to offer allegiance to the newly created Serb republic of BiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is: On the 27th of May of 1992, did you ask Mayor Pasic when was this new Serb Republic of BiH created?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specifically asked him when was the BS Republic created as it was the first time that I ever heard of the name, and yes, he proceeded to give me an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer was he wasn't sure when it began but -- let me quote it directly. This was in a meeting on the 27th of May. I'm sorry I am taking a little longer to ply through my notes. I know it's written somewhere. But to the effect that it was -- I'm sorry. I'm taking --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of what he said in substance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was before -- before the recognition of Bosnia. I'm missing that part, whether it was recognition of Bosnia or prior to our arrival in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very tired and now I miss giving all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But do you have a clear memory that when you asked Mr. Pasic when was the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina formed, he said it was formed before the recognition -- the international recognition of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm doubting. That's what I'm trying to recall, whether it was before our arrival or before the recognition of Bosnia. I know there was language to that effect that I noted down, and for some reason I am unable to locate it in my notes right now. But it was prior to the recognition of Bosnia, if I was to guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you clear in your memory of that, that he said it was before the international recognition of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subject to confirmation that I can't give you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, I'm sorry, just before you sat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please, could you read from your diary.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, Can't say -- and I quote, when I asked him: "Can't say when the government was formed but was before the international recognition of BH."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if we accept Mr. Pasic's assertion that you recorded there, then the events precipitating this mass exodus of Muslims from Northern Bosnia into Sector North occurred or began prior to the international recognition of Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a valid inference to make out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've asked plenty of questions, and the time has come to allow this witness to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an objection to make to you, Mr. May, and the question raised by the Prosecutor or, rather, the alleged Prosecutor. Questions of this type, when I ask them, you qualified them as being legal ones, legal matters, and you said that the witness wasn't competent enough to answer legal questions, and you can't look at legal questions without looking at the facts. So you put the facts down on one side and the legal questions on the other, parallel. And I wish to remind you that I asked the witness yesterday about the aggression on the part of the Croatian forces from the territory of the Republic of Croatia onto the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the region of the Bosanski Brod municipality on the 26th of March, 1992, when the massacre was performed of the whole village of Srpski Sijekovac, which was when the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke out. Up until that time, it was peaceful in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So legal issues of this type --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is all this? He wasn't being asked to make any kind of legal finding there. Now, we really must allow this witness to go. No. We're not going to go on arguing about this. Mr. Kirudja, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness have his diaries back. Unless you want them for any reason, he should have them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Dr. Bosanac. I'm very anxious that she may be concluded today. She's a paediatrician, and I think still the director of a hospital. She was here for, I think, five or more days, waiting to give evidence when the accused was last unwell. Her evidence is in -- in chief, her evidence is substantially given by former testimony in another trial, which the Chamber has admitted. I'm in the Chamber's hands as to precisely how we should deal with that. My proposal would be that we can, simply by headline and in order to give context to her evidence overall, identify in the summary provided the paragraphs that are dealt with in prior testimony, if that would be acceptable to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm afraid that I doubt we're going to finish her evidence today, given the time now. We have to be out at quarter to because there is another case coming in, quarter to two. We can't sit any longer than that. The sensible course may be to give the transcript an exhibit number. We have had the opportunity of reading it, so it can be taken very shortly, but I have to say the evidence took an hour and a half, at least, in the previous hearing, because there was a break towards the end of it, and therefore, I would anticipate that cross-examination will have to be of about the same length. So I'm afraid we're not going to finish her evidence today however desirable it would be. But in terms of the evidence in chief, you can take it that we've read it and you can take it quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I imagine the witness is being called for at the moment, so I'm not wasting time in explaining what we're doing. Also, it's hoped that the remainder of the evidence relating to Vukovar, of which this witness speaks, or much of it, may be produced by provisions of 92 bis, and accordingly, although I know Your Honour has, I think, probably considerable knowledge of the overall circumstances of Vukovar, I'm going to produce through this witness some maps and a video which will give context or better context for the other evidence that will or may come in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I believe that all of this and everything I got before is absolutely impossible for a cross-examination that would take place only an hour and a half. I will remind you that last time I said that, you said that you would bear it in mind if the cross-examination has to pertain to the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, no. We haven't ruled on the time. I was merely dealing with it in context of finishing the evidence today, and I said an hour and a half in terms of the transcript. Now, it may be that there will be further evidence and further time will be allowed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your full name Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A Croat by nationality, born in 1949 in Subotica in Serbia, you qualify as a doctor specialising in paediatrics and becoming the director of the Vukovar General Hospital on the 25th of July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to ensure that those viewing elsewhere fully understand how the evidence is being given, you gave evidence in a former trial, in an earlier trial at this Tribunal, and the transcript of that evidence has been allowed to be, in part, your evidence-in-chief. And may it now be convenient to give it an exhibit number, remembering perhaps to reserve one exhibit number from the document to be produced for the previous witness and to be produced overnight, if I understood the Chamber correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure I've got that. Which is the document outstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I thought you said in relation to one of the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. They're Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They're Defence exhibits, very well. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The transcript, Your Honour, will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 379.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I'm going to summarise, really, by headlines, Doctor, matters that have been covered in the evidence you gave to the Tribunal on an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. earlier occasion. You dealt with the ethnic composition of Vukovar; 43 per cent Croats, 37 per cent Serbs, 19 other minorities. Paragraph 3. During the war with which we are concerned, how many people, roughly, remained in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In Vukovar, in total blockade after the 15th of August, there were about 15.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The area under Croat control was approximately what size?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: It was the centre of town, Borovo Naselje, and that is approximately 10 kilometres by 3 kilometres, along the right bank of the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were those 15.000, approximately, people of various ethnicities, and so far as you're concerned, did the two major ethnic groups, the Croats and the Serbs, suffer equally in the attack upon Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. They certainly suffered equally. Actually, both Serbs and Croats remained, along with many other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed was Vukovar encircled so that it was impossible for goods or people to get in or out?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber will know, of course, that Vukovar can be seen on page 23 of its atlas, an area it would have been looking at regularly. For possible use by way of detail, we're going to add three exhibits to the map file. First, Exhibit 326, tab 15. If we can hand that in. Lay it on the overhead projector. It's an aerial photograph so it's a bit odd, but it's designed to give the geographical position in a little more detail. This shows the Danube, and we can see Vukovar Hospital on, of course, the west bank but north of the town centre. We can see the JNA barracks marked further to the south. So may that become 326, tab 15, with the following map 326, tab 16. This gives a more detailed view of the oblong shape of the Vukovar Hospital, located where we saw in the previous map. We'll come back to details of the hospital in photographs later. Thank you very much. Exhibit 326, tab 17. This shows the area of the Vukovar Hospital ringed, the river to the north and east, and a route which becomes significant later leading out to the south-west from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are those maps, Doctor, so far as you can understand, all accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, paragraphs 4 and subsequent, did you deal with how Vukovar Hospital was first shelled on the 15th of August of 1991 with artillery shells coming from Borovo Selo? Did you deal with how, on the 24th of August, a JNA car hit a land-mine so that soldiers were injured who were brought to your hospital for treatment, two of them being, I think, in such condition that they couldn't really be moved but subsequently they were taken away by soldiers at the insistence of the JNA? Is that correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The day after those soldiers were taken away, paragraph 6, did the JNA bomb the hospital for the first time, despite its being marked with a large red cross on the roof and another one in linen on the cross in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You could tell that the shelling came from positions held by the JNA on the other side of the Danube, and also from Negoslavci and Borovo Selo, the JNA planes flying over the hospital almost daily from the 14th of September to the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included in the bombs was the one that exploded at the second floor and one that crashed right through several floors but didn't actually explode, these being substantial bombs weighing 400 to 450 kilogrammes each?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously a terrible situation in Vukovar. Cluster bombs and bombs with phosphorous were used and your hospital was receiving up to 90 wounded persons a day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The hospital was undefended. There were wounded soldiers there but no fighting men, and weapons were removed from people when they came into the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By November 1991, Croatian soldiers brought three wounded JNA soldiers to the hospital. You spoke to General Raseta on the telephone, asking him to stop shelling the hospital, and one of those soldiers got on the phone with the general to tell him that the hospital was being shelled. Raseta said that he'd try to do something about it but nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You couldn't get supplies of medicines because of the forces surrounding the city. There were inevitable food shortages. Doctor, did you protest to the outside world about what was happening at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, every day. I sent appeals and protests, asking for deblockade, for help, for having the shelling of the hospital stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make those protests to the JNA, as we've already heard, and to an aide of the JNA Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As well as to General Raseta, the JNA commander in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able still to make telephone and fax communication with the outside world?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, until the 15th of November, I could send faxes. I could make telephones all the way up to the very end, until I was taken prisoner on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included -- included in the range of people to whom you made communication, was there Lord Carrington, Mr. Genscher, and Mr. van den Broek?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I sent my appeals and requests for help to the European Monitoring Mission in Zagreb, and I asked the politicians who had the -- who had major influence over war and peace in Yugoslavia then, to receive copies of those faxes. I asked the mission to forward the faxes to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a book been now published, copies available for the Chamber and translation provided of all those letters that haven't already been translated or written in English. There's a book, isn't there, Doctor, containing the appeals that you sent out during that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is to become -- I'm sorry. I have the wrong document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 380.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I don't know if you have -- could we just lay the actual hard copy of the book, if we've got one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I just see the time. Are you going to be many minutes with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to be very many minutes with it, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, it may be convenient, if the Court will indulge me in the interests of saving time, if the court, over the short break, would find an opportunity to glance at the book just for its general format and I can take you to a couple of pages after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Dr. Bosanac, we're going to adjourn for 20 minutes. Could you please remember in this and any other adjournments not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar has to correct some numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, with regards to the maps Exhibit 326, tab 15 which is a map depicting the Vukovar area with marked sites of Vukovar Hospital and JNA barracks should be tab 16. The tab previously marked tab 16 should be tab 17, and previously marked tab 17 should be tab 18. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Grateful. My error in naming them in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, we return to the communications you had with the outside world. The Court now has the exhibit numbered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have a number 380, have we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 380. If the Chamber has had an opportunity to look at it over the break, you will see it is a composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hold up the original. We have a couple of copies available. If you want to see the originals...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be helpful to have the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hand that in. The reason we're producing it not as originals is (a) there are a limited number of the originals, and (b), not every page was translated into one of the languages of the Tribunal. So maybe that can be part of the exhibit, although note that it's not absolutely complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The registry can have this one in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, we can see from this book that's produced that you were writing letters of complaint and concern and requests for help, or they were being written on your behalf, from October -- 20th of October certainly, right the way through to the end, I think, November of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I flagged one entry for showing on the overhead projector, please. If you could do that. First of all show the original Croatian version on the overhead projector so we can see what we're looking at. And the Chamber will note -- it's about half, two-thirds of the way through, and it's ERN number is 72539 at the top. What we can see is that on this letter there is some handwriting and apparent signatures before we reach the foot of the page. If you could hand that copy, please, to the doctor and then put on the overhead projector the following page in English. We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this, dated the 7th of November, to the European mission in Zagreb, sets out the position in the hospital. Tanks shells from the garrison. Third paragraph, endangering of newborn babies, and so on. Fourth paragraph: "I asked for urgent cease-fire and the withdrawal of JNA from the region of the municipality of Vukovar and outside of heavy artillery range." "For the verification of truthfulness for Mr. Raseta and all others that are responsible for this massacre on the hospital, I ask the wounded JNA soldiers to confirm with their signatures." And the writing we saw on the other page was indeed the writing of a JNA soldier from Nis, Mikovic Srdjan, and a JNA soldier from Belgrade, Jovan Sasa, and a JNA reserve from Sombor, Teofanic Pavle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did they sign this letter because of the position in which you and they found themselves?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move just to have a look at how the -- how the hospital appears at least nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Photographs of the hospital the next exhibit, please. And -- this needs a new exhibit number, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit 381.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are three photographs. I think if you just look at the first one first on the overhead projector. Does this show the hospital - we've already seen its oblong shape - as reconstructed after the war?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, a little difficult to see on this photograph, is there a driveway, an in and out for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... later. Just look at the next photograph, please, which shows that same driveway from one position and then the last photograph shows it from another. So that shows the view from the back and we can now see the driveway on the right. And then the third photograph. That actually shows the driveway itself, looking out. As I say, we will see the significance of that later. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the video booth now be good enough, please, to play us the video of the hospital. This also needs a new exhibit number, I think. And there's no transcript but perhaps the witness can tell us the odd thing about it as we go through it, and I'll ask her some questions to stimulate that narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, Doctor, what we're looking at as we're seeing it, please.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: We are actually looking at the evacuation of wounded persons in an ambulance. This is the entrance into the hospital. This is the corridor underneath the anti-atomic shelter on the right-hand side, and the door that leads to the anti-atomic shelter can be seen. This is the anti-atomic shelter where the most serious patients were after surgery. We see here the corridor again, the one in front of the shelter where the wounded persons were. This is what the building of the hospital looked like in 1991 before it was reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give a precise date for the taking of this video or not? It doesn't matter if you can't.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: It can be seen here when this bomb exploded on the second floor where surgery is. So it was after the 5th of October, but I cannot give you the exact date. This is the interior of the hospital building on that particular floor, after the bomb fell. This is the hall in the basement, which is also big. Here the crater can be seen, the one that went through all five floors of the hospital. This is the big bomb that weighed 450 -- 450 kilogrammes, but it did not explode. It fell on a bed in which a patient was lying. Some of the doctors can be seen here at one of our staff meetings. This is the interior of the hospital. The date can be seen here, that is, the 17th of October -- or, rather, the 5th of October. The 5th of October. That is the exact date when that bomb fell. It can be seen here exactly how it fell and how it broke that bed. The hole can be seen in the ceiling now, that it fell through.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see a British journalist. And we -- what do we see here then with the British journalist now around?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: These are some nurses and staff members who are getting the patients ready for evacuation. At that time, I was no longer at the hospital, but I saw these video clips. We see here how some patients and some civilians are setting out, how the evacuation is starting. Most of them are women, actually. Women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you say, this was after, as we're going to discover, you had been taken away and imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This happened on the 20th, Wednesday, in the morning, when I was taken from hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From the presence of the man in the white suit, Martin Bell, we can see that journalists were being allowed some view of what was going on by this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 20th of November, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And here? Can you help us with this?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: These are corpses of the persons who were killed over the past days, that is, those who were not buried yet in that period. But they were killed during the occupation. I can see that because of this child. This is the red cross that was in the hospital yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, returning to the summary, returning indeed to the former testimony and putting matters in a little more context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, on the 17th of November, did the JNA hospital shelling the hospital, as you said in your previous testimony, and in November were there some 250 wounded persons and more than a hundred old and sick people in the hospital at that time, along with mothers and their newly born babies and so on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You arranged an evacuation and, by telephone with the Croatian Ministry of Health's Dr. Hebrang, did you arrange for an evacuation to start on the 18th of November, you being informed that terms of evacuation had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that agreement is the only annex to the testimony in the prior hearing and can be found at the last page of Exhibit 379, or the last page but one. And again, as it's part of the prior testimony, I don't need to go into it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, a specific route and specific terms were agreed for the evacuation. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That agreement was signed in Zagreb at the European Monitoring Mission. The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the person who did not sign the agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the side of the Yugoslav army, it was Andrea Raseta, General Andrija Raseta, and on behalf of the Croatian government, it was Minister Andrija Hebrang. The hospital should have become neutral on the basis of that agreement on the 18th of November in the morning at 8.00 a.m., but three teams were supposed to come, of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And their position and again, because it's in your previous testimony we can deal with it briefly: The teams didn't come, you contacted General Raseta again, he advised you to talk to a Colonel Mrksic. You were told that the ICRC representatives and the JNA were at a bridge close to the hospital. You went to that bridge to try and lead the relevant people to the hospital, but when you got to the bridge you saw, instead, JNA soldiers and people you describe as Chetniks, forcing other people out of their homes and loading them onto the trucks that were available, and a local JNA commander knew nothing of the location of the ECMM or ICRC people who would be organising the evacuation. So you returned to the hospital, as your prior testimony reveals, when a jeep showed up, asking you to go to Negoslavci, which the Chamber can find on page 23 of its atlas, a few kilometres south of Vukovar, due south. You went to that town or village to a private house where you saw Colonel Mile Mrksic, whom you -- with whom you discussed the problem. Eventually, he agreed to an evacuation. You returned from there to the hospital to wait for that evacuation to happen. On the way, you saw a white van belonging to the ECMM, and you were taken back to the hospital. When you got back to the hospital, you sent someone to look for your parents-in-law. They were found and brought to the hospital, although your father was subsequently taken prisoner and his was one of the bodies found in the mass grave at Ovcara, to which we will turn briefly later. Of course, everyone in the hospital was by now scared because of numerous soldiers now present and there being no ICRC people around, the hospital being guarded by the JNA. In your hospital, were representatives of the local Red Cross. You visited all floors. There was panic. You went down to calm people, and you met a man called Major Sljivancanin, and this was, I think, the first time you'd seen him. And you saw civilians being taken out of the hospital, loaded onto a truck. You asked Sljivancanin what was happening, he said the plan was to evacuate first the wounded and then the civilians, saying that they were being taken to Velepromet. You protested because the ICRC and the ECMM were not present, but Sljivancanin took no notice of your protests. That's all covered in your prior testimony, and is it correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At about 7.00 in the evening, Sljivancanin came to your office with a man from the ICRC, apparently called Mr. Nikolas, Sljivancanin asking for a list of the wounded, of which he was given copies, as was Mr. Nikolas who said he'd come back the next day. Were you taken by the same JNA officer again to Negoslavci that evening, and when you got there did you see Sljivancanin who said that Colonel Mrksic was not there because he was on another assignment, there was somebody else there in authority - there was an exchange you can deal with - where Sljivancanin asked you how much President Tudjman would pay for you. You were taken to a school building and held prisoner overnight. On the 20th of November, you were taken back to the hospital. By now you were not allowed to use your telephone because there was a JNA officer there with a rifle. Sljivancanin came in at 7.00 in the morning, ordered you to call a meeting of medical personnel whom he then addressed, you complying despite saying you wanted to wait for the ICRC representative. That same soldier who had taken you to Negoslavci came in, saying that he had orders to take you and Marin Vidic for negotiations with the ICRC, although this turned out to be entirely untrue. And as you were led out from the hospital, we saw how the driveway in and out comes from one side to the other of the hospital, as you went out one way, what did you see happening -- what was happening at the other side of that runway or driveway?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: What I saw was a large number of hospital staff. They were waiting there, preparing for the evacuation. A nurse asked me where they were taking me, and I said to the negotiations and that I would be back quickly, but I left, never to return. They didn't allow me to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were taken, as a result of the misleading information you'd been given, not for negotiations but to the JNA barracks that we've already seen indicated on a map in the southern part of the town, I think, where you were kept in a room for the whole day. So you were unable to see what was going on at the hospital or to complain or object. And then at 6.00 in the evening, you were told that there had been some changes and that the ICRC had already done the evacuation. You were held overnight and the following morning you were taken to Sremska Mitrovica. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. During the night, that's when they took us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now see an existing exhibit, which is short. We've seen it once before. It's Exhibit 342, tab 10, the video of Vukovar bridge showing Sljivancanin. The Chamber may want to remind itself at some stage from its maps that there are two bridges, the one visible from another, and Sljivancanin has his back to a bridge. He's standing on one bridge, he has his back to another bridge at which the ICRC man is pointing, and the evidence will show that at the time of this discussion, the convoy of those being taken from hospital was passing by on the other bridge. If we can have a look at it again. There is also one point at which I may stop the video to draw to your attention a particular soldier in a helmet. His identification will be provided by the next witness I am to call, but if I show -- identify who it is now, it won't be necessary to play the whole video the next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have some sound track for this, please? And, Your Honour, there should be a transcript with the original exhibit which I hope has come to you. If not, there's further copies coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Freeze frame, please. The person I'm going to invite the Chamber to focus on is the person who can be seen in the bottom left-hand corner of the screen at the moment and who we'll have in a slightly better profile and slightly fuller face a little later. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've got the wrong transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The correct one coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's enough of that video. It's been seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, is the tall man with the moustache, talking, Sljivancanin who you've seen on a couple of occasions in circumstances described in your prior testimony?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was I right in what I suggested to the Judges at the beginning, that the view to the left, the view that would have been available to the man from the ICRC, was of another bridge, the bridge upon Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which, as we understand it, the people from the hospital were taken when they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now look, please, at the next video to be given a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, of course --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We teach and train all of our soldiers and our superiors that it represents great humanity and great honour to help every man and every nation. All in all, sir, this is about a dirty war which has not been conducted like this in history before. The Yugoslav People's Army -- the Yugoslav People's Army has emerged from the people's army which fought alongside the allies against the fascists in World War II. "The men that were in here, they go home to their families

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "No. Our soldiers are all together on their positions. They participated together only in action in liberation of the town of Vukovar. "[Indiscernible] "Can we make arrangements with people in northern command to go and see the hospital? I think that right now I cannot provide that. "Maybe somebody else can. "That can be solved, because in that part where there is a crossing across the Vuka river between us and the Operational Group North there are minefields, and we're not sure we're leading you where it is not safe for you. And we have not done the demining of those minefields yet. "We're not going to take you there. "Well, let me talk to my colleague [indiscernible] Let's first go downtown and -- "After he visited the army barracks, he spent some time in Negoslavci. Here he talked to the commander of the Operational Group, Colonel Mileta Mrksic and members of his staff. "This is the village of Negoslavci. Three kilometres south of Vukovar. "I see."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, at the time that those events were filmed -- you've been able to put things together, of course, since in your mind and work it out. At the time those events were filmed, were you already detained?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sljivancanin, of course, is the same man we've seen before. The Mrksic who was having the discussion with Cyrus Vance, is that the same man you'd seen in discussions when you'd been taken twice to Negoslavci? He was there, I think, once.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, subsequent witness will be able --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got an exhibit number for that video?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video of the hospital with no sound is Prosecutor's Exhibit 382. This video of the encounter of the Vukovar bridge is Prosecutor's Exhibit 383 -- no, excuse me, video of the evacuation is Prosecutor's Exhibit 383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you tell me the date of Mr. Vance's visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's the 19th of November, but the doctor can probably, from her recollection, tell us with more authority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 20th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wednesday the 20th, at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As I say, we have a later witness who was a party to some of those negotiations who will be able to assist us. Not negotiations; talks, meetings. Paragraph 31 of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Doctor, you were held a prisoner in Sremska Mitrovica and also in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For how many weeks were you detained?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the course of your detention, what did you observe of the questioning treatment and appearance following interrogation of fellow prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: On the first day, I was in a solitary confinement cell, and then with -- in another room with 60 other women from Vukovar, and the last days I was at the military investigation prison in Belgrade for two days. Then they took me off for questioning, and when they were bringing me back from questioning, I saw people who had been beaten up, and I heard cries and screams and lots of beatings going on during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your husband was also held in prison camps in Serbia, including at Sremska Kamenica and Stajicevo?
