utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how was he treated, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: He was very brutally treated. He had a lot of fractures to the ribs, and bruises, and he was beaten over the head, and he was in a coma the whole day. And he is suffering serious repercussions from the Kamenica period, and Stajicevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband and I visited Lord Carrington in -- we insisted -- we prevailed upon him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you speak up, you're asked by the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband went with me to see Lord Carrington, and I insisted for -- that -- that he ask Mr. Milosevic to allow Vukovar to go free. My -- we learnt that our relatives had been killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to that --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: So that Lord Carrington knew about the camp at Stajicevo, but unfortunately, they didn't release the people. Those who survived were released in the spring and summer of 1992, not before then. And many people were killed. And 400 persons from Vukovar are still listed missing. We don't know where they are. 396, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The movement of the people who were known to have been killed at the Ovcara farm is shown, Doctor, is it not, on two plans and some photographs that we've produced, and with your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If these two plans could be produced in order. The first one -- if this could be given a number, put on the overhead projector, subject to a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you understand it, the route from the hospital for those taken to the Ovcara farm and killed goes through the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. We're not looking at the right one. The other one first, please. The hospital first, just so that we -- can this one have that first number for logical or is that too difficult? This shows the route from the hospital, across the bridge where Sljivancanin was standing on the other bridge, parallel to it, and then down to the JNA barracks. And then the other plan which we looked at first, if we can put that one on now, shows the route from the barracks down to the Ovcara hangar and eventually, for those who were killed, to the gravesite. Perhaps both plans could have the same number. Would that be convenient? No. Right. I'll leave the registry to sort that out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map showing the route will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 326, tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will see that there are numbers, identification numbers given at various points along that route. The next exhibit is an album of photographs. Go through this very quickly. I'm not inviting the Chamber to do it now but you can connect the numbers on the bottom right-hand corner of those photographs with the places on those maps in case it becomes material to know how these people were taken. It starts off, photograph number 1, with the hospital. The photograph number 2 is on the way to the bridge. Photograph number 3 is again on the way to the bridge. Photograph number 4 is really at the bridge. We can see the bridge railings on the right. Photograph number 5 is a little bit south of the bridge on the way -- I beg your pardon. Photograph number 5 is also the bridge, as is photograph 6, showing how one bridge would give a view to another. And photograph 7. Photograph number 8 shows part of the route south of the bridge towards the barracks. Photograph number 9 the same. And photograph 10 and 11. And then we come -- after that one, please. Next photograph, please. And the next one. Here we are now at the barracks where people, as you understand it, Doctor, were held for some time. Similarly, the next photograph and the one after that. Then we come -- next photograph, please. And the next. This is the route from the barracks down towards the farm. The other chart now relates, and we can follow a route - next photograph, please - across the countryside. Next photograph, please. Next photograph. Next photograph. We're now at the first sightings of the Ovcara hangar. Next photograph, please. Closer view of the hangar. Next photograph. And the next. This is the hangar where people were held, now with agricultural equipment in it. Next photograph, please. And the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the last photograph shows the route from the hangar which - last photograph, please - shows the route from the hangar, top left, down the photograph, turning to the right along to one of the gravesites that, as you understand it, Doctor, was the scene of some of the burials of those killed at Ovcara farm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to remind the Judges, is it a question of all those who were taken away being found in that grave or are there a large number completely unaccounted for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: A large number was taken away in six buses, six busloads, in fact. All those people were taken away. But in the grave, 200 dead bodies were found of which only 186 have so far been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last exhibit, please, which is an annex --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a number for the photographs, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photographs, Your Honour, will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 384.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last exhibit, which I forecast may become Exhibit 385, is pages 44 to 50 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last exhibit is pages 44 to 50 of the Croatian indictment, but now highlighted in blue, yellow, and green.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've marked this list of names, Doctor, or had it marked at your direction. What's the meaning of blue?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The ones marked in blue were the employees of the then-medical centre Vukovar. Most of them were drivers or handymen and they were taken away that morning too in those buses, together with some wounded, and they were identified at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nineteen of them. Did you identify any of them yourself or are you dependent for your evidence on the identification of others?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Those people, the ones who were killed at Ovcara in 1995 were identified in the mass grave in 1996. They were taken for -- to the medical faculty in Zagreb for forensic examination, and the family members were called there too. They were looking for their nearest and dearest, looking for their family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The nineteen blue employees marked by the witness. Turning to yellow, these are children under the age of 18. One, two, three, four of those. And the green are your family members, and we can see two of those. Explain, please, about your family members who were killed there. You already mentioned your father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, my father-in-law was waiting to be evacuated from the hospital, together with my mother-in-law and my mother. He was old and infirm, and it was difficult for him to sit around the whole night. A soldier of the Yugoslav army passed by the hospital and said that all those who were able to walk should go outside. He went outside to stroll around and see when the evacuation would take place, and when he left the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. building, he was sent off into one of the buses, and he never returned until we identified him. He was killed at Ovcara. As for the other relation of ours, Tomislav Bosanac, he was a civilian, and he was accompanying his wife, who was seriously wounded. She was a nurse and barely managed to survive. I asked Major Sljivancanin whether I could take my family members out together with the wounded hospital staff and all the other wounded persons, and he said that I could. He allowed me -- he said I could, but this relation of ours was also taken off and killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Bosanac. Thank you for permitting me to take the evidence swiftly. You will be asked some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we see what really happened in Vukovar, tell me, is it correct that members of the National Guards Corps of the Croatian army and police were staying at the hospital in larger numbers and firing at the JNA from there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, your colleagues, doctors who were with you in the hospital at that time, say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness can't deal with that. The witness doesn't know what other people say. You will have to deal with her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am dealing with her evidence, but I want her to comment upon something that his -- her colleague stated. For example, I have it here, Mr. May, in the court record of a witness hearing that I believe should be shown to this particular witness here so that she could perhaps remember whether what she has been saying was correct or not. For example, Mladen Ivankovic, your colleague, head of surgery, who was heard as a witness before a court said that from the moment when five wounded Serbs came who were guarded by members of the Croatian MUP, that is to say from the beginning of May 1991 until these events that you were speaking about, all the time there were members of the National Guards Corps and the MUP at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was director of that hospital, and I know exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He says: "They did not go out until the liberation of the hospital on the 19th of November, 1991." Also, he says that in hospital there were between 100 and 150 armed men. In the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that. Let the witness deal with that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely. That is absolutely incorrect. The medical staff were at the hospital, including Dr. Ivankovic. Also there were wounded persons, patients, and other assistants. There were two men from the police. One was Tomislav Hegedus, who was recording the dead, and the other one was Branko Lukinda whose task was that when wounded Croatian soldiers came in, he would take their weapons and carry them to the building of the police. So in the hospital, there were absolutely no weapons or armed Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that this is incorrect, that there were between 100 and 150 armed soldiers in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to exhibit this court record later, but I have a few questions related to that in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to consider that. This Dr. Ivankovic, what ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Serb, actually from Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And was he at the hospital throughout this siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Actually, he tried to run away and then he was wounded, and then they returned him again, wounded. I asked my staff not to leave the hospital because it was very dangerous. Hundreds of shells were falling on the hospital every day, and I asked that nobody go out. Five staff members from the hospital were killed before the occupation, by shells. Nineteen were killed at Ovcara. Three are still missing. And we also have information that five civilians and nurses were killed after the occupation. Among the 300 persons who were killed after the occupation of Vukovar or, rather, 300 non-Serbs and Croats who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know anything about -- well, let's bear in mind the fact that as a witness before the court, he was duty-bound before the law to speak the truth, that guards members came during the night armed, they had sniper rifles. They went up to the roof of the hospital. They returned from the roof during the night. Sometimes it was in the morning when a bomb fell on the hospital. He said: "We were informed that before that somebody was shooting at aircraft from the roof of the hospital." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is absolutely not true. Dr. Ivankovic worked as a surgeon, and he was in the basement of the shelter all the time. And I claim with full responsibility that armed soldiers never went up to the roof of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In addition to the roof that he refers to, he says in the front of the hospital from the park and from the yard of Electro Slavonija near the hospital, members of the ZNG were targeting JNA positions, engaging their gunfire -- their guns. Then shells fell and some hit the hospital as well. Is that correct, what he says?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: It is not correct. From the surroundings of the hospital, there was not a single gun, a single cannon of the Croatian army or the ZNG that was firing. That is correct. But what is correct is that every day hundreds of shells and aircraft bombs were falling on the hospital itself or on its immediate surroundings. One shell hit the room where these soldiers of the Yugoslav army were. And every day, over 70 or 80 shells fell on the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember when Dr. Kust [phoen], an ethnic Croat, is that right, an anaesthesiologist who came from Zagreb, he asked you to prohibit people from shooting from the hospital roof?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's a record of that as well.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's not true. You can or, rather, the Court can, if they wish, call Dr. Kust. That is not correct, because nobody ever shot from the roof of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This Dr. Ivankovic - I'm moving on to Dr. Ivankovic again now after referring to Dr. Kust, because he speaks about that in his own statement - did he ask you to do something about this, to stop that, to stop people from firing from the hospital? And you kept saying that only a few more days should be taken or, rather, three more days and then everything would be resolved. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Dr. Ivankovic asked me to do something, to call the barracks in order to stop the firing at the hospital. I did call the barracks of the Yugoslav army, like many other evidence that has been presented here, but no one ever shot from the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Your colleague Dr. Vladimir Emedi [phoen], so this is also a non-Serb, and he also worked at the hospital at that time, he said that you allowed for weapons to be brought into the hospital. And in connection with that, he also cautioned you against that. I have his statement too that was given to investigative authorities. He says: "As the director of the institution, she allowed weapons to be brought into the hospital. After being cautioned by colleagues that weapons should be taken away, she did not do a thing." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That is not correct. I said that wounded soldiers had their weapons taken away. And Dr. Emedi, like many other doctors who were non-Serbs, was arrested and he was staying at the prison in Nis. I don't know what he said there under duress and what kind of pressure was exerted against him, but he works at the hospital now, and if necessary, he can make a statement to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He also says that people with weapons were climbing up on the roof of the hospital and targeting aircraft from there and they were killing people as snipers.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a rocket targeted an aircraft from your hospital and it was after that that the aircraft targeted that roof?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. That is absolutely not true. The aeroplane targeted the Vukovar Hospital on the 25th of August for the first time, the Vukovar Hospital. And there were no weapons whatsoever at the hospital. You can get many testimonies to that effect. The ones that you have are obviously tendentious and incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These are official documents, Mrs. Bosanac. I'm reading from them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you are putting, Mr. Milosevic, is some statement made by a witness to a totally different court. It's another statement which you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This statement was given by Dr. Vladimir Emedi on the 29th of November to the investigative Judge of the military court, Major Zvonko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was he a prisoner? Do you know that, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I know that, because he and his father were released together with me on the 10th of December. They were in a camp in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was being subjected to interrogation, is that right, as you would understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The name of Borislav Kucan, does that mean anything to you? Thirteen days before Vukovar fell, he left town. He was there.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He is one of the snipers who was shooting at people from the roof of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No. Absolutely incorrect. And you could not leave town 13 days beforehand because nobody could leave town, but he certainly did not shoot from the roof of the hospital. That name is quite unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Quite unknown to you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Emedi says the few times three trucks came with Red Cross signs, the usual size, they were driven by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They told us that they brought ammunition, weapons, and on one occasion -- oh, I should read slower. Right, yes. So the truck with the sign of the Red Cross, regular size, that was driven by Dr. Josip Husar [phoen], Obradovic Zupa [phoen], and Josip whose heel had been injured, they told us that when they came in, they brought ammunition, weapons, and on one occasion, even cannons. According to their statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're in fact going beyond time. Do you know anything about what is being said here, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of September, Dr. Josip Husar would come to evacuate wounded persons in a Red Cross truck. These were big trucks that could take in 12 to 16 wounded persons. They came to the hospital, we would prepare the wounded, and they would take the wounded out of Vukovar. I don't know what they brought in. I didn't see that. And that is how they kept coming until the end of September. After that, Vukovar was completely occupied and nobody could come in or go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have to call it a day there since the Court is required. Mr. Milosevic, we've considered the time you should have. We will give you two hours, up to two hours more for cross-examination tomorrow. Dr. Bosanac, I'm sorry we haven't been able to finish your evidence today. Could you be back tomorrow to conclude it at 9.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
